stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman at 27+5 weeks gestation attends her local diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic for her routine screening 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. She is asymptomatic. Her booking weight gave a BMI of 29 kg/m2, she gained 4 kg in her last pregnancy with a 3.8 kg baby and no GDM diagnosed retrospectively, and she has no family history of type 2 diabetes. Her previous antenatal visits have been unremarkable. She fasted from midnight as instructed.

Her test results have just come back to the clinic registrar.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5°C
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 28 cm; fetal heart 142/min; no oedema
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting glucose 5.3 mmol/L; 1 hour 11.4 mmol/L; 2 hour 8.0 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and immediate management?

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes on the 1 hour value and start carbohydrate-counted dietary advice with home glucose monitoring.
Report the test as normal and repeat screening only if fetal macrosomia develops on subsequent ultrasound.
Repeat the entire OGTT at 32 weeks to confirm the diagnosis before instituting any treatment changes.
Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately without trialling lifestyle modification first.
Order an HbA1c above 6.5 percent threshold to confirm gestational diabetes before any further action.

subtopic_detail: Counselling on what intrapartum prophylaxis does and does not prevent
stem: A 30-year-old woman colonised with group B streptococcus is in early labour at 40 weeks and has had her first intravenous dose. She asks what the antibiotic will do for her baby.

data_table.Labour: Cervix 4 cm, membranes intact, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Antibiotic: First dose given 20 minutes ago with no reaction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate explanation?

options.text: It lowers infection in the first week but not illness appearing later
It removes any risk of infection from this organism in the first month
It works by clearing the organism from her birth canal within the hour
It protects mainly against infection appearing after the first week
It is given for her own risk of infection rather than for the baby

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P3 woman is 25 minutes postpartum following a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with active third stage. Estimated blood loss is now 1100 mL and ongoing from the placental bed; the placenta is complete on inspection. She was treated for gestational hypertension during pregnancy with labetalol 200 mg twice daily and her blood pressure on the labour ward 30 minutes before delivery was 158/108 mmHg. Bimanual compression has been started and a second 16 G IV cannula is in. Oxytocin 10 IU IM has been given as part of active third stage and an oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1000 mL Hartmann's at 250 mL/hr has been running for 15 minutes.

The consultant is asking what to add next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122/min, blood pressure 156/104 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy at the umbilicus, blood loss from below ongoing; perineum intact; bladder catheterised and empty
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L (115-165); platelets 142 x10^9/L; INR 1.1; fibrinogen 2.6 g/L; cross match in progress
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg bd; oxytocin infusion running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological agent?

options.text: Ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscularly together with tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously.
Misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually as a single dose with no additional intravenous therapy.
Carbetocin 100 micrograms intravenously as a single bolus dose to replace ongoing oxytocin therapy.
Recombinant activated factor VII 90 micrograms/kg intravenously before any further uterotonic doses.
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes plus carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly.

stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 34+5 weeks gestation has been admitted with severe headache, visual scotomata, and right upper quadrant pain. Her booking blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg and BMI 24. Two readings 15 minutes apart in triage have been 168/112 mmHg and 162/110 mmHg. Antihypertensive therapy has been commenced with oral labetalol 200 mg and her blood pressure 30 minutes later is 152/96 mmHg. She has 3+ proteinuria on dipstick, normal fetal movements, and a reactive CTG. The on-call obstetrician has decided to deliver in the next 24 hours after a course of betamethasone.

The team is now discussing seizure prophylaxis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 152/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C, fetal heart 145/min reactive
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes with 2 beats of clonus bilaterally; mild epigastric tenderness; no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 96 x10^9/L; ALT 72 U/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L; urate 0.42 mmol/L; LDH 320 U/L; PCR 320 mg/mmol
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg orally given; betamethasone 11.4 mg IM started

lead_in: What is the most appropriate magnesium sulfate regimen?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading dose over 20 minutes then a maintenance infusion of 1 g/hour.
Magnesium sulfate 6 g IV loading dose over 20 minutes followed by a 2 g per hour maintenance infusion.
Phenytoin 18 mg/kg intravenous loading dose given over 30 minutes for eclampsia seizure prevention.
Oral nifedipine 30 mg modified release alone, deferring magnesium until a seizure actually occurs.
Diazepam 10 mg intravenously as a single dose with onward titration of labetalol infusion only.

stem:
A 29-year-old G2P0 woman presents to early pregnancy assessment at 7+3 weeks from her last menstrual period with 3 days of mild left iliac fossa pain and minor brown vaginal spotting. She is haemodynamically stable. Her last serum beta-hCG taken at the GP 48 hours ago was 2200 IU/L and today it is 2850 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterine cavity with thin endometrium, a 22 mm left adnexal mass with no fetal pole and no cardiac activity, and a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her FBC, renal function, and liver function are within normal limits. She has no significant past history, takes no medications, and lives nearby with reliable transport.

She is keen to avoid surgery if possible and has been counselled about the options.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 80/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, no cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 48 hour rise 2200 to 2850 IU/L; TVUS left adnexal 22 mm mass, no FH; small free fluid; Hb 132 g/L; LFTs and creatinine normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta-hCG every 48 hours until the value has spontaneously declined.
Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with follow-up beta-hCG on day 4 and day 7.
Diagnostic laparoscopy with planned salpingectomy of the affected fallopian tube during the same procedure.
Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 plus prophylactic folate 5 mg orally daily for 7 days.
Emergency theatre for salpingectomy on the basis that any free fluid signals a tubal rupture.

stem:
A 27-year-old G1P0 woman with a monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancy at 22+5 weeks gestation is reviewed at the fetal medicine unit after an outside scan reported amniotic fluid discordance. She has felt well; no antepartum bleeding or contractions. The current detailed scan with paired Doppler studies has just been reported by the maternal-fetal medicine consultant. Both fetuses have normal anatomy. Twin A (the donor) is structurally normal with deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm; twin B (the recipient) has deepest vertical pocket 9.2 cm with a visible bladder.

Umbilical artery Dopplers and ductus venosus traces are also reported.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, fundal height 28 cm; cervix on TVUS 36 mm and closed
data_table.Investigations: Twin A EFW 380 g; bladder not visualised; DVP 1.4 cm; UA Doppler with absent end-diastolic flow. Twin B EFW 540 g; visible bladder; DVP 9.2 cm; UA Doppler normal; ductus venosus normal a-wave

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Amnioreduction from the recipient sac alone every 7 days until 28 weeks gestation is reached.
Expectant management with weekly Dopplers because absent end diastolic flow alone can be transient.
Refer urgently for fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the placental vascular anastomoses.
Selective feticide of the donor twin by bipolar cord coagulation to maximise recipient survival.
Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly and plan delivery within 48 hours by caesarean.

stem: A 31-year-old primigravida at 32+2 weeks presents with new severe headache and right upper quadrant pain. Booking blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg. Today her blood pressure is 168/112 mmHg after 30 minutes of rest. She has had three doses of oral nifedipine 20 mg over 90 minutes with blood pressure now 152/98 mmHg. CTG is reassuring. Bloods: platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 96 U/L (5-35), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), urine protein-creatinine ratio 86 mg/mmol. Fetal growth was at the 25th centile two weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 152/98 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8°C, FHR 140
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes, no clonus, mild RUQ tenderness, no peripheral oedema documented
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 92, ALT 96 U/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, urate 0.42 mmol/L, urine PCR 86 mg/mmol; CTG normal variability with accelerations
data_table.Medications: Nifedipine immediate release 20 mg PO x3 over 90 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Expectant management until 37 weeks with twice-weekly bloods, CTG and growth scan
Discharge home on oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily with weekly review
Plan delivery within 24-48 hours after IV magnesium and antenatal corticosteroids
Proceed to immediate emergency caesarean before any steroid loading dose
Continue oral nifedipine and add aspirin 100 mg daily for preventive effect

stem: A 34-year-old G2P1 has had a normal vaginal delivery of a 4.1 kg infant after a four-hour second stage. Active management of the third stage was performed with oxytocin 10 IU IM. Twenty minutes after the placenta the uterine fundus is boggy at the umbilicus and 900 mL of blood has been lost. She has been catheterised, the placenta is reported as complete, no genital tract trauma is identified, and there are no clots in the vagina. She had blood pressure 158/104 mmHg in late pregnancy and is on oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily. Current blood pressure is 132/88 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 132/88 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Examination: Fundus boggy at umbilicus, ongoing trickle PV, perineum intact, placenta reported complete
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 900 mL and rising; Hb pending
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin 10 IU IM (third stage), labetalol 200 mg TDS PO, IV access secured with 1 L Hartmann's running

lead_in: Which uterotonic is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IM ergometrine 250 micrograms with prochlorperazine 12.5 mg for nausea
Misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingual after one further oxytocin infusion bolus
IV tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes as the sole pharmacological action
IM carboprost 250 micrograms while preparing for theatre balloon tamponade
IV magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus to relax associated arterial spasm and clot

stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 39+1 weeks attends the birth suite reporting a 'gush' of clear fluid 14 hours ago. She is not in labour. Vaginal speculum confirms pooling of clear amniotic fluid. The cardiotocograph is reactive. Her group B streptococcus swab at 36 weeks was negative. She has had no fevers and reports normal fetal movements. She tells you she would prefer to go home and 'see if labour starts on its own'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C, FHR 138
data_table.Examination: Speculum confirms amniotic pooling, no offensive discharge, cervix appears 1 cm dilated visually
data_table.Investigations: GBS negative at 36 weeks; CTG reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.text: Discharge home with a thermometer and review in 48 hours if not in labour
Commence oxytocin infusion now in the birth suite with epidural insertion
Insert a Foley balloon for cervical ripening and start prophylactic ampicillin
Recommend caesarean section now for prolonged rupture exceeding 12 hours
Offer induction now or within 24 hours of rupture with inpatient monitoring

stem: A 26-year-old G2P1 at 19+4 weeks attends fortnightly ultrasound for a known monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancy. Today the recipient twin's deepest vertical pocket is 8.6 cm and the donor twin's deepest vertical pocket is 1.4 cm. Both bladders are visible, umbilical artery Dopplers show normal end diastolic flow in both, and venous Doppler waveforms are normal. Both growth percentiles are on track for gestation. Maternal observations are normal and she reports a tight abdomen but no contractions.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C, no contractions on tocograph
data_table.Investigations: Twin A (recipient) DVP 8.6 cm, bladder visible, normal Dopplers; Twin B (donor) DVP 1.4 cm, bladder visible, normal Dopplers; growth concordant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to a fetal medicine unit for assessment and laser candidacy
Continue fortnightly scans and review at the next routine appointment
Perform serial amnioreductions weekly to control polyhydramnios in recipient
Plan elective caesarean delivery at 32 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids
Start maternal sildenafil 20 mg three times daily to improve donor perfusion

stem: A 32-year-old G4P0 presents two weeks after her third consecutive first-trimester loss. All three losses occurred between 8 and 11 weeks, two were ultrasound-confirmed missed miscarriages, and one was a complete miscarriage at home. Her menstrual cycles are regular at 28 days. She has no history of thromboembolism, no family history of miscarriage, and no chronic disease. Karyotyping of the most recent products of conception showed 46,XX with no aneuploidy. She is otherwise well and asks what investigations are appropriate now.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24, no acanthosis, no goitre, no hirsutism
data_table.Investigations: Cycle history regular; recent products of conception karyotype 46,XX

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line investigation panel?

options.text: Inherited thrombophilia panel including factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene
Pelvic ultrasound with antiphospholipid screen and thyroid function tests
Endometrial biopsy with natural killer cell quantification and HLA typing
Parental karyotyping for both partners and routine sperm DNA fragmentation
Empirical low-dose aspirin and LMWH from positive pregnancy test next cycle

stem: A 33-year-old G2P2 was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 28 weeks during this pregnancy and was managed with diet alone (no insulin or metformin). She has now had an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery of a healthy 3.6 kg baby at 39+5 weeks. She is six weeks postpartum, breastfeeding, and her finger-prick glucose readings have been 5.6 to 6.4 mmol/L fasting at home. She has no symptoms of hyperglycaemia. She asks what monitoring she needs going forward.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27.4, no acanthosis nigricans, breastfeeding established
data_table.Investigations: Pregnancy: GDM diagnosed at 28 weeks by 75 g OGTT (fasting 5.4, 1h 11.2, 2h 8.8 mmol/L), diet controlled; postnatal: home fasting glucose 5.6 to 6.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What follow-up plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Repeat 75 g OGTT only at the start of any subsequent pregnancy as routine
Annual fasting plasma glucose only and reassess if she conceives again
75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum and HbA1c every 1-3 years thereafter
Commence metformin 500 mg daily empirically to prevent type 2 diabetes
Refer to endocrinology now for insulin initiation given fasting near 6 mmol/L

stem: A 16-year-old presents with oligomenorrhoea (cycles every 70-90 days for the last 2 years), mild facial hirsutism (Ferriman-Gallwey 10), and acne unresponsive to topical therapy. She is not sexually active. Body mass index 28.5. Bloods: total testosterone 2.8 nmol/L (0.5-2.4), SHBG 28 nmol/L (30-90), TSH 1.6 mU/L, prolactin 240 mU/L, 17-OH progesterone 4 nmol/L, fasting glucose 5.3 mmol/L. Pelvic ultrasound is reported as showing more than 20 small follicles per ovary. She wants help with cycle regulation and acne. Her mother is concerned about long-term endometrial protection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: BMI 28.5, Ferriman-Gallwey 10, comedonal and inflammatory acne over face and back
data_table.Investigations: Testosterone 2.8 nmol/L, SHBG 28 nmol/L, TSH 1.6 mU/L, prolactin 240 mU/L, 17-OH progesterone 4 nmol/L, fasting glucose 5.3 mmol/L, more than 20 follicles per ovary on ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Spironolactone 100 mg daily without concurrent contraception cover
Metformin 500 mg twice daily as monotherapy for menstrual regulation
Cyclic medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg for 10 days every 3 months
Combined oral contraceptive containing 30 mcg ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel
Letrozole 2.5 mg daily on cycle days 3-7 to induce ovulation each month

stem: A 29-year-old G3P3 is seen at her six-week postnatal review. Her delivery was an uncomplicated normal vaginal birth. She is fully breastfeeding and her baby has not been formula-supplemented. Her menstrual periods have not returned. She is in a stable relationship and asks about a copper intrauterine device because she does not want hormonal contraception. She has no history of pelvic infection or heavy menstrual bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Uterus involuted, lochia minimal, no offensive discharge, perineum healed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to gynaecology theatre for insertion under general anaesthesia next month
Defer copper IUD insertion until 12 weeks postpartum to reduce expulsion
Recommend condoms only and review again in six months for the IUD
Start the progestogen-only pill today and insert copper IUD at six months
Insert the copper intrauterine device today after current pregnancy is excluded

stem:
A 30-year-old G3P1 at 32 weeks' gestation presents after a 200 mL painless fresh vaginal bleed at home. The bleed has now stopped. Her anomaly scan documented a complete placenta praevia. Her blood group is A positive. The fetus is moving normally and CTG shows a reassuring trace with baseline 140 bpm, variability 10 bpm, accelerations present, no decelerations. Speculum was deferred. Bedside ultrasound confirms cephalic presentation and placenta covering the os. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (115-165) and platelets 198 x10^9/L (150-400).

The maternal fetal medicine team is on-site.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C, fetal HR 140
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no uterine tenderness, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 112 g/L, platelets 198 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 4.2 g/L, blood group A positive; ultrasound complete praevia, cephalic, normal EFW

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit, betamethasone IM, cross-match 2 units, and plan caesarean at 36-37 weeks
Discharge home with safety netting after 4 hours of observation
Immediate category 1 caesarean section regardless of fetal status
Induction of labour with vaginal prostaglandin and aim for vaginal birth
Outpatient management with twice-weekly midwifery review and aspirin 100 mg

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P2 has just delivered a healthy 3.8 kg infant by emergency caesarean at 39 weeks for failure to progress. Her BMI booking weight was 41 kg/m^2. She has no personal or family history of VTE. The operation was uncomplicated with an estimated blood loss of 600 mL. She has no current bleeding and her blood pressure has returned to baseline. She has not received any anticoagulation. Her platelet count is 220 x10^9/L (150-400) and her creatinine is 64 micromol/L (45-90).

The postnatal ward team is preparing her discharge medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Wound clean and dry, uterus contracted, lochia minimal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L, platelets 220 x10^9/L, creatinine 64 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate VTE prophylaxis plan?

options.text: Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for 6 weeks postpartum
Aspirin 100 mg orally daily for one week as sole prophylaxis
Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for 10 days only
Mechanical prophylaxis with calf compression and mobilisation
Apixaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily for 6 weeks postpartum

stem:
A 28-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks is admitted in spontaneous labour. After artificial rupture of membranes a midwife feels a pulsating loop of cord through the cervix. The cervix is 4 cm dilated and the fetal head is at -3 station. CTG shows variable decelerations to 70 bpm with slow recovery. The bedside theatre team has been activated and the obstetric consultant is en route. The mother is in the antenatal ward bed.

The team has been briefed and she gives full consent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 128/74 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8°C, fetal HR 70 (decelerations)
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, fetal head -3 station, pulsating cord in vagina
data_table.Investigations: CTG variable decelerations to 70 bpm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action while waiting for caesarean?

options.text: Knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg, elevating the presenting part
Cover the cord with warm saline-soaked gauze and otherwise leave undisturbed
Push the cord back into the uterus and start oxytocin to expedite delivery
Insert catheter and infuse 500-750 mL into bladder for transfer
Start magnesium sulfate 4 g IV bolus to suppress contractions

stem:
A 33-year-old G3P2 at 34 weeks presents with sudden severe constant abdominal pain that began two hours ago. She reports no vaginal bleeding. She is normotensive with mild tachycardia. The uterus is tense and tender between contractions. CTG shows a sinusoidal pattern with reduced variability and late decelerations. Maternal haemoglobin is 92 g/L (115-165), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2.0-4.5), INR 1.4 (0.9-1.2). Ultrasound shows a retroplacental clot with no praevia.

The team has been briefed and consent obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.8°C, fetal HR sinusoidal
data_table.Examination: Tense tender uterus, no external bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L, platelets 88 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.4 g/L, INR 1.4; ultrasound retroplacental clot

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Category 1 caesarean section with massive transfusion protocol activation
Tocolysis with nifedipine and steroids, plan delivery at 36 weeks
Induction of labour with oxytocin aiming for vaginal birth
Conservative management with continuous CTG and serial coagulation
Cryoprecipitate alone targeting fibrinogen >2 g/L, then reassess delivery

stem:
A 32-year-old G1P0 at 40 weeks has been pushing for 30 minutes. The head delivers but retracts firmly against the perineum and external rotation fails. McRoberts hyperflexion has been performed and suprapubic pressure applied for 30 seconds without delivery. Estimated fetal weight at 38 weeks was 4.0 kg. The mother is fully dilated. The shoulders remain impacted. CTG had been reassuring until head-on-perineum sign.

The team is in position around the bed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102, BP 134/84 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.9°C, fetal HR not currently auscultatable
data_table.Examination: Fetal head retracted against perineum, external rotation failed
data_table.Investigations: Cervix fully dilated; fetus presumed cephalic

lead_in: What is the next most appropriate manoeuvre?

options.text: Rubin II internal rotation by pushing the anterior shoulder forward
Symphysiotomy under local anaesthetic to widen the pelvic outlet
Apply axial traction with stronger maternal pushing efforts
Zavanelli manoeuvre with cephalic replacement and immediate caesarean
Fundal pressure to drive the anterior shoulder under the symphysis

stem:
A 36-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks presents with progressive shortness of breath for ten days, two-pillow orthopnoea, and bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. She has no history of cardiac disease. There is no chest pain. Echocardiogram shows global LV hypokinesis with LVEF 28%, no valvular lesion, and a moderate pericardial effusion. NT-proBNP is 5400 ng/L (normal <300). CTG is reassuring. She is currently in spontaneous early labour with the cervix 3 cm dilated, fetus cephalic, no membrane rupture.

Multidisciplinary delivery planning is in progress.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 106/64 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 94%, temperature 36.7°C, fetal HR 140
data_table.Examination: Raised JVP 5 cm, bibasal crackles, bilateral pitting oedema, S3 gallop
data_table.Investigations: LVEF 28%, NT-proBNP 5400 ng/L; CTG reassuring; cervix 3 cm dilated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Assisted vaginal birth under epidural with shortened second stage
Immediate category 1 caesarean section under general anaesthetic now
Nifedipine tocolysis and elective caesarean section at 40 weeks
Bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily to delay delivery for optimisation
Insert intra-aortic balloon pump pre-emptively before delivery

stem:
A 30-year-old G1P0 at 33 weeks presents with right upper quadrant pain and nausea for 18 hours. She has had no previous antenatal hypertension. Examination shows tender liver edge. Urine dipstick 3+ protein. Bloods: haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-165), platelets 40 x10^9/L (150-400), AST 380 U/L (0-40), ALT 410 U/L (0-40), LDH 920 U/L (140-280), creatinine 102 micromol/L (45-90), uric acid 0.48 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), fibrinogen 2.8 g/L. INR 1.0. Blood film shows fragmentation. CTG is reassuring.

The team has been briefed and consent obtained for delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 168/108 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C, fetal HR 142
data_table.Examination: RUQ tenderness, hyperreflexia, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L, platelets 40 x10^9/L, AST 380 U/L, ALT 410 U/L, LDH 920 U/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, urate 0.48 mmol/L, fibrinogen 2.8 g/L, INR 1.0; film fragmentation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for delivery and anaesthesia?

options.text: Caesarean under GA after labetalol, magnesium, and platelets >50
Epidural and assisted vaginal birth after platelet transfusion
Spinal anaesthesia without platelet transfusion at current platelet count
Conservative management with steroids; reassess delivery at 48 h
Induction of labour with oxytocin and IV pethidine for analgesia

stem:
A 29-year-old G1P0 attends her 26-week antenatal appointment after her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. She has been well, is gaining weight along expected centiles, and has no symptoms. Her booking BMI was 26 kg/m^2. She has no family history of diabetes and is not on any regular medications.

Her fasting plasma glucose was 4.8 mmol/L. The 1-hour value was 10.4 mmol/L. The 2-hour value was 7.8 mmol/L. Her HbA1c at booking was 5.0%. Her urinalysis today is negative for glucose and protein.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 100%, temperature 36.6 °C, fetal HR 145 bpm
data_table.Examination: Fundal height appropriate for dates, normal symphysis-fundal growth chart, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting 4.8 mmol/L, 1-hour 10.4 mmol/L, 2-hour 7.8 mmol/L, booking HbA1c 5.0%, urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?

options.text: Normal glucose tolerance because the fasting and 2-hour values are below threshold
Gestational diabetes diagnosed on the 1-hour OGTT value alone, no repeat needed
Repeat the OGTT in 4 weeks because only one value is elevated on this test
Pre-existing type 2 diabetes because the HbA1c at booking was above 5.5%
Impaired glucose tolerance only, not gestational diabetes, on these OGTT values

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P0 presents to the early pregnancy unit with 2 weeks of intermittent right iliac fossa discomfort. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She has no syncope, no shoulder-tip pain, and no significant bleeding. She lives 20 minutes from the hospital and can attend twice-weekly follow-up.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 3.1 cm right tubal mass without fetal cardiac activity and no free fluid. Beta-hCG is 4200 IU/L. Her LFTs and UEC are within normal limits. She has had no prior abdominal surgery and no contraindications to methotrexate.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 100%, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, mild right adnexal tenderness, no peritonism, no cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: TV ultrasound 3.1 cm right tubal mass, no fetal cardiac activity, no free fluid, beta-hCG 4200 IU/L, UEC and LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management option?

options.text: Emergency laparotomy with salpingectomy regardless of haemodynamic stability
Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the right tube as definitive surgical management
Laparoscopic salpingostomy with conservation of the right tube and bhCG follow-up
Expectant management with serial beta-hCG and no methotrexate or surgery
Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m^2 with serial beta-hCG monitoring

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P2 presents on day 4 after a forceps-assisted vaginal delivery with a 12-hour history of fever and lower abdominal pain. She had prolonged rupture of membranes (28 hours) before delivery. Her lochia is heavy and foul-smelling.

On arrival to the postnatal ward she is alert and orientated. There is no calf swelling, no respiratory symptoms, and no flank pain. The uterus is tender on bimanual examination at the level of the umbilicus. Initial bloods show a raised CRP and a left shift on FBC.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98%, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Tender boggy uterus at umbilicus, foul-smelling lochia, no calf swelling, chest clear, mild suprapubic tenderness without peritonism
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.4 × 10^9/L (4-11), CRP 145 mg/L (<5), lactate 1.8 mmol/L, urine MCS sent, blood cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Computed tomography abdomen and pelvis prior to starting any antibiotic therapy
Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily as outpatient treatment for 7 days
Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g eight-hourly as broad-spectrum monotherapy
Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg load then 15 mg/kg twelve-hourly as monotherapy
Intravenous amoxicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole until afebrile for 24 hours

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P1 is seen in the antenatal clinic at 32 weeks gestation to discuss mode of delivery. Her first pregnancy was 3 years ago at 35 weeks for severe early pre-eclampsia. The operation note from that admission records 'extension of lower segment incision required, vertical extension up the uterine body, repaired in two layers'.

This pregnancy has been uncomplicated. The fetus is cephalic, AFI 14 cm, EFW 50th centile. Placenta is fundal. She has been counselled about VBAC versus elective caesarean and asks for your advice.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 100%, temperature 36.6 °C, fetal HR 142 bpm
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 32 cm, cephalic presentation, no scar tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound at 32 weeks: fundal anterior placenta, AFI 14 cm, EFW 50th centile, fetal Dopplers normal

lead_in: Which feature is the strongest absolute contraindication to attempting VBAC?

options.text: Estimated fetal weight on the 50th centile at 32 weeks gestation review today
Maternal age 34 with a body mass index of 28 kg/m^2 at booking visit
A single previous lower-segment caesarean section in the immediately prior pregnancy
Previous classical (vertical) uterine incision documented in the operation note
Past medical history of severe early-onset pre-eclampsia in the first pregnancy

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 at 40+2 weeks is brought into the birth suite by ambulance with spontaneous rupture of membranes 30 minutes ago. Her previous two pregnancies were uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. She declined external cephalic version at 37 weeks because she was not comfortable with the procedure. Her last ultrasound at 38 weeks showed a footling breech.

On arrival vaginal examination reveals 4 cm dilated cervix with a foot palpable below the cord and no cord prolapse identified. CTG is reassuring at baseline 140 bpm. The on-call obstetrician and paediatric team are present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6 °C, fetal HR 140 bpm
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, footling breech with right foot palpable through cervix, no cord prolapse, contractions every 4 minutes
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound confirms footling breech, EFW 3.6 kg, AFI 6 cm post-SROM, no nuchal cord visualised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Induction of labour with augmentation by oxytocin and continuous fetal monitoring
Vaginal breech delivery with epidural analgesia and experienced obstetric assistance
Emergency caesarean section as soon as the operating theatre is available
External cephalic version now under bedside ultrasound guidance after SROM
Internal podalic version with breech extraction by the on-call obstetric registrar

subtopic_detail: Refractory primary PPH escalation - mechanical tamponade vs surgical
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P3 woman has delivered a live male infant by spontaneous vaginal birth. She had a precipitate second stage. Within 15 minutes of delivery she has had brisk ongoing bleeding from the genital tract. She has already received: oxytocin 10 IU IM, ergometrine 250 micrograms IM, oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1000 mL Hartmann's at 250 mL/hour, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, and bimanual uterine compression for 10 minutes.

Vaginal and perineal lacerations have been sutured. The placenta is intact on examination. Estimated blood loss is now 1500 mL. She has no known medical conditions, no anticoagulants, no pre-eclampsia, and her blood pressure is currently stable on a unit of packed red cells running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 96/62 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 4 L/min, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy and soft despite uterotonics, ongoing brisk red bleeding per vagina, no expanding haematoma, perineum repaired and dry
data_table.Investigations: Hb 86 g/L (115-160), platelets 154 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 2.4 g/L (2.0-4.5), APTT and INR within normal limits, fibrinogen falling on serial samples
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin infusion, tranexamic acid given, one unit packed red cells running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a Bakri intrauterine balloon and inflate to tamponade while preparing theatre
Transfer to interventional radiology for uterine artery embolisation now
Repeat ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscularly with monitoring of blood pressure
Proceed straight to B-Lynch compression suture under anaesthesia in theatre
Give intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms and repeat once in 15 minutes

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic with prior contralateral salpingectomy - surgical choice
stem:
A 31-year-old G3P1 woman, last menstrual period 7 weeks 2 days ago, presents with right iliac fossa pain and a small amount of dark vaginal spotting. She had a left tubal ectopic pregnancy 2 years ago treated by laparoscopic salpingectomy. She has been trying to conceive for the past 12 months and this is her first positive pregnancy test since the salpingectomy. She had a postpartum tubal contralateral preservation note in her previous operative report.

Her obstetric team has reviewed her. The on-call gynaecology consultant has had a detailed antenatal discussion of the choices with her partner and her present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, no rebound, cervical os closed
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 4200 IU/L, transvaginal ultrasound shows a 28 mm right tubal mass with no fetal cardiac activity, no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, empty uterus, the left adnexa shows surgical absence of the tube as expected, anti-D negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingostomy with conservation of the tube
Laparoscopic right salpingectomy with planning for future IVF
Methotrexate 50 mg/m^2 intramuscularly with weekly serial beta-hCG
Expectant management with serial beta-hCG every 48 hours
Laparotomy and total abdominal hysterectomy with right salpingectomy

subtopic_detail: HELLP syndrome with thrombocytopenia - delivery and anaesthesia decision
stem:
A 28-year-old G2P0 woman at 34 weeks 2 days presents with a 2-day history of right upper quadrant pain. She has known pre-eclampsia treated with oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily since 32 weeks. Magnesium sulfate was loaded 1 hour ago and a maintenance infusion at 1 g/hour is running. Fetal heart rate is normal with reactive CTG.

Decision-to-deliver has been made and platelet count has dropped on serial samples over the last 6 hours. The on-call anaesthetic registrar has been called and the consultant obstetrician is in the unit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102, BP 165/110 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal HR 145 reactive
data_table.Examination: Right upper quadrant tender to palpation, hyperreflexic with 3 beats of clonus, no scotomata reported
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L (115-160), platelets 64 x10^9/L (150-400, was 110 four hours ago), LDH 820 U/L (<280), AST 240 U/L (<35), ALT 198 U/L (<35), bilirubin 38 micromol/L (<20), INR 1.0, fibrinogen 3.4 g/L (2.0-4.5), uric acid 0.46 mmol/L (<0.36), urinalysis protein 3+
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg PO TDS, magnesium sulfate infusion 1 g/hour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anaesthetic and delivery plan?

options.text: Continue expectant management at 34 weeks with daily inpatient monitoring
Administer high-dose intravenous dexamethasone to delay delivery for 48 hours
Augment labour for vaginal delivery under epidural analgesia today
Proceed to category 2 caesarean section under general anaesthesia urgently
Caesarean under spinal anaesthesia after platelet transfusion to above 100

subtopic_detail: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome Quintero staging - laser timing
stem:
A 27-year-old G1P0 woman with a monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancy at 19 weeks 4 days is referred from her local fetal medicine unit. The amniotic fluid volume has changed rapidly over the last 2 weeks. She has been previously well.

The maternal fetal medicine consultant has reviewed the ultrasound and the staging discussion has just concluded. Both fetuses appear structurally normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart rates both reactive
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus consistent with 24 weeks size, no contractions, cervical length 32 mm
data_table.Investigations: Monochorionic-diamniotic twins. Twin 1 (donor): deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm, empty bladder, umbilical artery Doppler with persistent absent end-diastolic flow. Twin 2 (recipient): deepest vertical pocket 10.4 cm, visible distended bladder, normal umbilical artery Doppler, normal ductus venosus a-wave, no hydrops

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Maternal sildenafil 20 mg three times daily to improve uteroplacental flow
Selective fetal reduction of the donor twin by radiofrequency ablation
Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses
Serial amnioreduction every 1 to 2 weeks until viability is reached
Conservative observation with weekly Doppler velocimetry studies

subtopic_detail: HELLP syndrome and timing of delivery
stem:
A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 32+3 weeks gestation is admitted to the high-risk obstetrics ward with right upper quadrant pain and headache. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated. She has no chronic hypertension. Her booking BP was 110/70 mmHg. She had no prior obstetric admissions this pregnancy. She received antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone) for fetal lung maturity 14 hours ago after her platelet count began to fall.

Over the last 6 hours her platelets have dropped further despite stable BP control with oral labetalol. She remains alert and oriented. Cardiotocograph shows a reassuring trace.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 146/94 mmHg (on labetalol), RR 18, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate 145 bpm with reactive trace
data_table.Examination: Right upper quadrant tenderness without peritonism, 3+ proteinuria on dipstick, no clonus, normal reflexes, no facial oedema
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 62 x10^9/L (down from 95 6 hours ago, baseline 220), AST 320 U/L (<35), ALT 280 U/L (<35), LDH 820 U/L (<250), haemoglobin 96 g/L with schistocytes on film, creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L (<0.36), urine PCR 580 mg/mmol
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg PO TDS, magnesium sulfate IV (loading 4 g + 1 g/hour maintenance), betamethasone 11.4 mg IM doses x 2 (last dose 14 hours ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue expectant management with daily bloods until 34 weeks then plan delivery
Increase the labetalol dose and continue magnesium sulfate, review at 12 hours
Transfuse a single adult dose of platelets and continue expectant management
Commence intravenous heparin for presumed HELLP thrombotic microangiopathy
Plan delivery within 6 to 12 hours by the most appropriate route after steroids

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 19+5 weeks gestation with a monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancy is referred to a tertiary fetal medicine centre after her routine fortnightly ultrasound. Her previous pregnancy was a term singleton delivery. She has no chronic medical conditions. First-trimester combined screening showed both fetuses with normal nuchal translucency and chorionicity confirmed as monochorionic-diamniotic at 12 weeks.

She has noticed increased abdominal girth over the past week. The fetal medicine consultant has reviewed her in clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus equivalent to 26 weeks size, soft, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound deepest vertical pocket of donor twin 1.2 cm (oligohydramnios less than 2 cm), deepest vertical pocket of recipient twin 9.4 cm (polyhydramnios greater than 8 cm); donor bladder visible; both fetuses with normal Doppler waveforms in umbilical arteries, middle cerebral arteries and ductus venosus; no hydrops in either twin; estimated fetal weight discordance 18%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses
Serial amnioreduction every 1 to 2 weeks until fetal lung maturity
Selective fetocide of the donor twin by bipolar cord coagulation
Continue fortnightly ultrasound surveillance with no intervention
Plan elective delivery by classical caesarean section at 28 weeks

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P0 woman at 32 weeks gestation is referred to a tertiary fetal medicine unit after her morphology scan and follow-up imaging. She conceived via IVF with a fresh embryo transfer. Her first pregnancy ended in a missed miscarriage at 9 weeks. The 20-week morphology scan reported a low-lying placenta with a succenturiate lobe; a follow-up transvaginal scan at 30 weeks confirmed a velamentous cord insertion with a fetal vessel running across the internal cervical os.

She is asymptomatic with no bleeding and good fetal movements. The maternal-fetal medicine consultant has reviewed her in clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no uterine activity, fundal height 30 cm, cervix long and closed on transabdominal assessment
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound with colour Doppler confirms a fetal vessel crossing the internal cervical os within 2 cm; placenta no longer praevia (lower edge 4 cm from internal os); estimated fetal weight 50th centile; reactive CTG; FBC, group and hold normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Continue routine antenatal care with delivery at 39 weeks unless labour intervenes
Inpatient admission 30-32 weeks with steroids and elective caesarean 34 to 36 weeks
Plan elective caesarean at 39 weeks with cross-matched blood and neonatal team
Perform an emergency caesarean today because vasa praevia is now confirmed on ultrasound
Outpatient weekly cervical length monitoring with planned vaginal delivery anyway

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 woman at 35 weeks gestation presents to the birth suite by ambulance with headache and visual flashing. Her booking blood pressure was 110/68 mmHg. She has had two BP readings at home of 165/108 and 168/110 mmHg this morning. She has had no proteinuria at previous antenatal visits. She has no chronic hypertension or other comorbidities. Her partner is with her.

On arrival she is anxious but oriented. The obstetric registrar is at the bedside and intravenous access has been established.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 168/112 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart rate 140 bpm reactive
data_table.Examination: 3+ proteinuria on dipstick, brisk reflexes with 2 beats of clonus, no facial oedema, no abdominal tenderness, CTG reassuring
data_table.Investigations: FBC haemoglobin 124 g/L, platelets 188 x10^9/L (150-400), AST 32 U/L (<35), ALT 28 U/L (<35), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.38 mmol/L (<0.36), urine PCR 220 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for acute blood pressure control?

options.text: Oral nifedipine immediate-release 20 mg given by the sublingual route as crisis dose
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus then 1 g per hour as the primary BP agent
Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus with repeat doses to a maximum 220 mg cumulative
Intravenous nitroprusside infusion titrated to a target BP under 140/90 mmHg
Oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily as a maintenance antihypertensive agent

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P3 woman has just had a vaginal delivery of her third child following a syntocinon-augmented labour for slow progress. The placenta delivered intact but soon afterwards she developed brisk fresh PV bleeding. Her uterus felt boggy. She is in the birth suite with the obstetric registrar and anaesthetic registrar at the bedside; the obstetric consultant has been called.

Over the last 25 minutes she has received IV syntocinon infusion, ergometrine 250 mcg IM, intramuscular carboprost 250 mcg, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, bimanual compression and a Bakri balloon inflated to 500 mL. She has bled approximately 2200 mL total and continues to bleed around the balloon at about 200 mL every 5 minutes. She has had 4 units of packed cells, 2 units FFP and 1 platelet pool transfused. Her perineal repair is intact. Theatre is being prepared.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 97% on 6 L/min via mask, temperature 36.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, uterus firm with Bakri balloon in situ, continued PV bleeding around the balloon, no perineal source
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L (post-transfusion, baseline 118), platelets 78 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 1.6 g/L (>2 intrapartum target), INR 1.6, calcium 0.94 mmol/L ionised (1.16-1.32), lactate 4.2; fibrinogen concentrate 2 g being prepared
data_table.Medications: Syntocinon 40 IU/L infusion, ergometrine 250 mcg IM, carboprost 250 mcg IM, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, packed cells x4, FFP x2, platelets x1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly as the fourth uterotonic dose
Transfuse an additional 4 units of packed cells before any surgical intervention
Insert a second Bakri balloon transvaginally on top of the existing balloon now
Transfer to theatre for examination and surgical haemostasis with IR backup if stable
Commence intravenous recombinant factor VIIa 90 mcg/kg as an off-label haemostatic

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman with diet-controlled gestational diabetes is in the second stage of labour at 39+5 weeks. Her previous pregnancy resulted in a 4.4 kg infant delivered vaginally without complications. Estimated fetal weight on a growth scan two weeks ago was 4.3 kg. Her labour has progressed normally and the head has just delivered with the chin pointing toward the maternal left thigh; the head retracts against the perineum.

Routine downward traction has failed to deliver the anterior shoulder. The midwife has called for help and the obstetric registrar is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate decelerating to 90 bpm
data_table.Examination: Head delivered, turtle sign positive, no anterior shoulder descent with maternal effort and routine traction, mother positioned in semi-recumbent
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable - this is an intrapartum emergency

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Apply suprapubic pressure and pull harder with fundal pressure to dislodge the shoulder
Cut a generous mediolateral episiotomy and continue routine downward traction now
Proceed immediately to deliberate clavicular fracture (cleidotomy) as initial step
Apply Zavanelli manoeuvre by replacing the head and proceed to emergency caesarean
Perform McRoberts manoeuvre (hyperflex maternal thighs) with suprapubic pressure

stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 35+6 weeks gestation with a twin pregnancy is admitted to the high-risk obstetric ward with a week of malaise, anorexia and nausea, and 3 days of right upper quadrant discomfort. She has been increasingly drowsy over the last 24 hours. She has no past medical history and her pregnancy was uncomplicated until now. Her BP at the last antenatal visit was 118/74 mmHg.

On admission she is jaundiced and sleepy but rousable. Her partner reports she has been confused about names of family members this morning. The obstetric registrar and gastroenterology registrar are at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 134/84 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.1 °C, fetal heart rates both reactive
data_table.Examination: Sclera icteric, jaundice on skin, mild RUQ tenderness, no peripheral oedema, mild asterixis, BSL 2.4 mmol/L, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: AST 580 U/L (<35), ALT 480 U/L (<35), bilirubin 142 micromol/L (3-20) predominantly conjugated, ALP 280 U/L, GGT 220 U/L, INR 2.4, fibrinogen 1.2 g/L (>2 intrapartum target), platelets 102 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 138 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.46 mmol/L (<0.36), urine PCR 80 mg/mmol, BSL 2.4 mmol/L (low), ammonia 110 micromol/L (<50), white cell count 16 x10^9/L, viral hepatitis screen negative, abdominal ultrasound shows hyperechoic liver with no focal lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stabilise hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy and arrange urgent delivery
Commence empirical N-acetylcysteine and admit to intensive care without delivery
Transfer for emergency liver transplantation assessment and continue the pregnancy
Diagnose HELLP syndrome and proceed to delivery after a course of betamethasone
Treat as fulminant viral hepatitis and isolate while awaiting hepatitis E PCR

stem:
A 32-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends her 28-week antenatal review. Her BMI at booking was 31 kg/m^2 and her mother has type 2 diabetes. The dating ultrasound and 20-week morphology scan were normal. She is otherwise well and on routine pregnancy vitamins.

She has returned today for the results of her 75 g oral glucose tolerance test performed at 27 weeks after an 8-hour fast. Her fasting plasma glucose is 5.4 mmol/L, 1-hour post-load 9.8 mmol/L, and 2-hour post-load 8.0 mmol/L. She has no symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia or weight loss.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height 27 cm at 28 weeks, fetal heart rate 142, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1), 1-hour 9.8 mmol/L (<10), 2-hour 8.0 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.Medications: Iodine 150 mcg, folic acid 500 mcg, vitamin D

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis and next step?

options.text: Normal test; reassure and continue routine antenatal care with no further glucose monitoring
Gestational diabetes; commence dietitian-led medical nutrition therapy with self-monitoring of blood glucose
Gestational diabetes; commence insulin glargine 10 units nocte immediately as the proposed approach
Type 2 diabetes overt in pregnancy; commence insulin and refer to endocrinology urgently
Borderline result; repeat the OGTT in 2 weeks before any diagnostic label as the proposed approach

stem:
A 24-year-old woman attends your GP clinic to discuss contraception. She has been on a combined oral contraceptive pill (ethinylestradiol 30 mcg / levonorgestrel 150 mcg) for the past 2 years with good cycle control. Over the last 6 months she has developed two episodes of unilateral visual scintillations lasting 20 minutes followed by a unilateral throbbing headache; her GP previously documented migraine without aura.

She smokes 3 cigarettes daily, BMI is 24 kg/m^2, blood pressure today is 122/78 mmHg, and her family history is unremarkable. She is sexually active in a monogamous relationship and wants long-term reliable contraception with low maintenance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular and neurological examination normal, no carotid bruit, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening up to date and normal; routine bloods within normal limits 6 months ago
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive ethinylestradiol 30 mcg / levonorgestrel 150 mcg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in contraception?

options.text: Insert a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system after counselling on insertion and bleeding patterns
Switch to a 20 mcg ethinylestradiol combined pill and review symptoms in 3 months
Continue current pill and add aspirin 100 mg daily for stroke prophylaxis as the proposed approach
Switch to the vaginal ring (etonogestrel/ethinylestradiol) and review in 3 months
Recommend condoms alone with cessation of all hormonal contraception as the proposed approach

subtopic_detail: Newborn care when intrapartum prophylaxis was incomplete
stem: You review a term baby on the postnatal ward an hour after a rapid spontaneous vaginal birth. The mother is colonised with group B streptococcus and remained afebrile throughout.

data_table.Antibiotic: One intravenous benzylpenicillin dose, given 90 minutes before the birth
data_table.Baby: Feeding, pink, temperature 36.9 degC, respiratory rate 48 /min, no recession

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the baby?

options.text: Clinical observations on the postnatal ward for at least 24 hours
Blood culture and intravenous antibiotics started now for 48 hours
Full blood count and C-reactive protein now and again at 24 hours
Surface swabs and a lumbar puncture before deciding about treatment
Routine postnatal care, with discharge at six hours if feeding well

stem:
A 29-year-old woman attends your fertility clinic with 18 months of primary infertility. Her cycles are irregular, occurring every 45 to 90 days with light flow. She has hirsutism on the chin and lower abdomen, acne, and her BMI is 27 kg/m^2. Pelvic ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries with multiple peripheral follicles bilaterally. Her partner's semen analysis is normal.

Day-3 hormonal profile shows raised LH:FSH ratio, mildly raised testosterone, and normal prolactin and TSH. Hysterosalpingogram demonstrates patent fallopian tubes. She has been counselled on weight optimisation and lifestyle changes for 6 months without conception.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: BMI 27 kg/m^2, Ferriman-Gallwey 12, mild acne, no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: FSH 5 IU/L (3-10), LH 14 IU/L (2-12), testosterone 2.6 nmol/L (<2.0), prolactin 380 mIU/L (60-560), TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), AMH 64 pmol/L (12-49); HSG patent bilateral tubes; partner sperm density 32 million/mL with normal motility and morphology

lead_in: What would you first recommend as ovulation induction therapy?

options.text: Recombinant FSH gonadotrophin injections from cycle day 3 with transvaginal ultrasound monitoring
Clomifene citrate 50 mg orally daily on cycle days 2-6 for up to six ovulatory cycles
Metformin extended-release 1500 mg daily as ovulation induction monotherapy
Letrozole 2.5 mg orally daily on cycle days 2-6 for up to six ovulatory cycles
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling as the initial ovulation induction approach as the proposed approach

stem:
A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends for her 11-week-plus-4-day dating ultrasound. The scan confirms a live twin pregnancy with two fetuses each measuring crown-rump length consistent with her last menstrual period. The intervening membrane meets the placental surface in a T-shape (no lambda sign), with a single placental mass and a thin intervening membrane. Both fetuses appear morphologically appropriate for gestation with present nasal bones and normal nuchal translucency measurements.

She is otherwise healthy with a BMI of 23 kg/m^2 and no significant medical or family history. She asks how her pregnancy will be monitored.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no visible scars
data_table.Investigations: Dating ultrasound 11+4 weeks: live twin pregnancy, T-sign at membrane-placenta interface, single placental mass, normal NT measurements bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surveillance plan?

options.text: Four-weekly ultrasound from 20 weeks with growth assessment and delivery at 37-38 weeks as the proposed approach
Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks with growth and amniotic fluid assessment, fetal Doppler studies and timed delivery at 36-37 weeks
Routine antenatal care as for a singleton pregnancy with delivery at 40 weeks with the proposed clinical action
Weekly cardiotocograph from 28 weeks with delivery at 34 weeks as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
Refer for early elective caesarean section at 32 weeks because of the chorionicity as the proposed approach

stem:
A 32-year-old woman with a 4-year history of endometriosis is referred to your clinic with worsening cyclical pelvic pain, dyschezia, and rectal bleeding with menstruation over the past 6 months. She has tried a combined oral contraceptive in continuous regimen and the levonorgestrel IUS without adequate symptom control. Her CA125 is 65 U/mL.

Pelvic ultrasound shows a 4 cm right ovarian endometrioma and a 2 cm bowel wall hypoechoic mass at the rectosigmoid junction with loss of the normal hyperechoic submucosal layer. MRI confirms a 25 mm full-thickness rectal nodule infiltrating the muscularis and approaching the mucosa, with a separate uterosacral ligament nodule.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Tenderness in the pouch of Douglas, fixed retroverted uterus, no palpable rectal mass
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound: 4 cm right ovarian endometrioma; 2 cm rectosigmoid bowel wall lesion. MRI: 25 mm deep infiltrating endometriotic nodule of anterior rectum + uterosacral nodule. CA125 65 U/mL (<35)
data_table.Medications: Continuous COC trial failed; levonorgestrel IUS trial failed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence GnRH agonist therapy with add-back tibolone as definitive management as the proposed approach
Refer to a tertiary endometriosis multidisciplinary clinic with colorectal and minimally invasive gynaecology input
Proceed with laparoscopic ablation of visible peritoneal endometriosis at the local hospital
Initiate aromatase inhibitor letrozole plus norethisterone as third-line hormonal therapy
Schedule total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy as first-line definitive surgery

stem:
A 34-year-old woman in her fourth pregnancy at 32 weeks gestation is referred to the maternal-fetal medicine unit. She has had three previous caesarean sections, all uncomplicated. Her current pregnancy was complicated by an anterior placenta praevia identified at the morphology scan. Detailed expert ultrasound at 28 weeks identified multiple placental lacunae, loss of the uteroplacental clear zone, retroplacental hypervascularity, and bridging vessels into the bladder. MRI confirms anterior placental tissue invading the bladder wall.

She is otherwise well, BMI 26 kg/m^2, has had a course of antenatal corticosteroids at 31 weeks, and her haemoglobin today is 124 g/L. She has been counselled on placenta percreta in the previous antenatal multidisciplinary meeting. She is asking when delivery should be planned, given she has small children at home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C, fetal heart rate 142
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, three lower-segment caesarean scars, fetal cephalic presentation
data_table.Investigations: MRI: anterior placental tissue traversing myometrium with bladder wall invasion. Ultrasound: lacunae, loss of clear zone, hypervascularity, bridging vessels. Haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-160), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 4.2 g/L, group A positive, antibodies negative
data_table.Medications: Iron supplement, antenatal corticosteroids course completed at 31 weeks

lead_in: What would you first recommend regarding timing and mode of delivery?

options.text: Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34-35 weeks gestation in a tertiary placenta accreta spectrum centre with interventional radiology standby, cross-matched blood, and pre-arranged urology input
Planned vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with active management of the third stage as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action as the proposed clinical action
Planned caesarean section at 39 weeks with manual removal of the placenta at delivery in the local maternity unit with the proposed clinical action
Emergency caesarean section today regardless of fetal lung maturity to avoid antenatal haemorrhage as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
Conservative management with methotrexate and leaving the placenta in situ after caesarean delivery, with serial bhCG follow-up as the proposed approach

subtopic_detail: HPV not 16-18 with LSIL reflex cytology
stem:
A 28-year-old woman attends your general practice clinic for results of her routine 5-yearly Cervical Screening Test. She has no abnormal bleeding, no postcoital bleeding, and no pelvic pain. She had a previous screening test 5 years ago that was negative. She is sexually active with a single male partner of 3 years, uses combined oral contraception, and has had no abnormal cervical results in the past. She is not pregnant.

Her current Cervical Screening Test reports oncogenic HPV detected (non-16, non-18 type) with reflex liquid-based cytology showing low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (possible LSIL). Speculum at sample-taking was unremarkable; the cervix appeared smooth and there were no contact-bleeding findings noted. She is up to date with her HPV vaccination history (3-dose schedule in adolescence). She asks 'do I need a biopsy now?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 116/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Speculum: cervix smooth, no friable lesion, no contact bleeding, no abnormal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Cervical Screening Test: HPV non-16/18 detected; reflex liquid-based cytology low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (possible LSIL)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat the Cervical Screening Test in 12 months irrespective of cytology grade or HPV genotype reported
Refer to a gynaecologist for diagnostic excisional biopsy (large loop excision of the transformation zone) within 6 weeks
Refer urgently to colposcopy clinic for diagnostic assessment and directed cervical biopsies within 8 weeks
Treat her empirically with vaginal imiquimod and repeat the Cervical Screening Test in 3 months
Repeat the Cervical Screening Test in 12 months and refer to colposcopy if HPV remains detected at that point

stem:
A 32-year-old woman attends your general practice clinic 4 months postpartum complaining of palpitations, tremor, weight loss of 4 kg despite a good appetite, and feeling 'hot all the time'. Her mother says 'she has been tearful and snappy, she's not herself'. She is breastfeeding and has not had a postnatal contraceptive review. Her last menstrual period before pregnancy was regular. She denies eye pain, double vision, or visual changes.

On examination she has a fine tremor of outstretched hands, a smooth non-tender symmetrical small goitre without bruit, and no proptosis or lid lag. There is no pretibial myxoedema. Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 9. Initial bloods show TSH 0.04 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), free T4 28 pmol/L (10-22), and free T3 9 pmol/L (3.5-6.5). She wonders 'is it just my hormones from feeding?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 regular, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, smooth small symmetrical goitre, no bruit, no proptosis or lid lag, no pretibial myxoedema, lactating
data_table.Investigations: TSH 0.04 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), free T4 28 pmol/L (10-22), free T3 9 pmol/L (3.5-6.5), EPDS 9; TSH-receptor antibody pending, thyroid uptake scan not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to clarify the cause?

options.text: Twenty-four-hour urinary iodine excretion testing before considering any further investigation steps
Repeat thyroid function tests in 4 weeks without any further immediate biochemical or imaging testing
Refer for radioactive iodine uptake scanning this week to differentiate Graves from thyroiditis
Order TSH-receptor antibody and TPO antibody titres in addition to a small thyroid ultrasound now
Commence empirical carbimazole 15 mg orally daily for biochemical hyperthyroidism while awaiting any further work

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum admission and refeeding risk
stem:
A 24-year-old gravida 1 para 0 woman presents to your emergency department at 9 weeks gestation with severe vomiting for 10 days. She tells you 'I can't keep water down for more than a few minutes'. She has lost 5 kg from her pre-pregnancy weight of 64 kg. She has had ginger, B6, oral metoclopramide, and ondansetron prescribed by her general practitioner without lasting effect. She has no abdominal pain, no fever, and no urinary symptoms.

On examination she has dry mucous membranes and a soft abdomen. Urinalysis shows ketones 3+ with no nitrites or leukocytes. Bloods show sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 90 mmol/L, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, urea 8 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L. Beta-hCG is appropriate for gestation; thyroid function is mildly suppressed (TSH 0.3 mIU/L). She has not eaten reliably for nearly two weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 100/60 mmHg standing 92/56 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, capillary refill 3 seconds, abdomen soft non-tender, fundus not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis ketones 3+; sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, urea 8 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L; beta-hCG appropriate for gestation; TSH 0.3 mIU/L; transabdominal ultrasound single live intrauterine pregnancy matched for dates
data_table.Medications: Ondansetron 8 mg orally (last dose 6 hours ago), metoclopramide PRN, ginger, pyridoxine 25 mg three times daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous thiamine, intravenous fluid with potassium replacement, then escalate antiemetics
Commence intravenous 5% dextrose 1 L over 1 hour with intramuscular cyclizine for symptom control
Discharge with oral doxylamine-pyridoxine combination tablet and outpatient antenatal follow-up next week
Arrange immediate termination of pregnancy referral given the severity of the maternal vomiting and weight loss
Commence high-dose oral prednisolone 60 mg daily before any intravenous fluid or thiamine is given to her

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida attends your antenatal clinic at 14 weeks gestation for routine review. She is well, with no urinary symptoms, no flank pain, and no contraction-like discomfort. Her booking-visit midstream urine culture has just returned: Escherichia coli at greater than 10^8 CFU/L, sensitive to nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim, cefalexin, and amoxicillin-clavulanate. She has no penicillin allergy and no other medical history. Booking renal function and blood pressure are normal.

On examination she is afebrile. Abdomen is soft with a fundus consistent with dates. Urinalysis at the clinic visit is now negative for nitrites or leukocyte esterase. She asks 'do I really need antibiotics if I feel fine?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, fundus consistent with dates, no renal angle tenderness, no costovertebral tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Booking midstream urine culture E. coli >10^8 CFU/L, sensitivities as above; today urinalysis nitrites and leukocyte esterase negative; routine antenatal bloods within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin including iodine and folate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that asymptomatic bacteriuria does not need antibiotic treatment in a healthy pregnancy and rescreen routinely
Commence oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days and repeat midstream urine culture 7 days post-treatment
Repeat the urine culture in 2 weeks before deciding whether antibiotic treatment is justified for this woman
Prescribe a single oral dose of fosfomycin 3 g once and arrange routine clinic follow-up at 6 weeks
Refer to obstetric medicine for inpatient intravenous antibiotic treatment regardless of symptom status today

stem:
A 24-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic with worsening cyclical pelvic pain for 3 years, dyspareunia for 6 months, and heavy menstrual bleeding requiring tampon and pad together with overnight changes. She tells you 'the pain takes over for the first 2 days every month and I have to call in sick'. She is currently not in a relationship and does not want pregnancy in the next 2 years, but would like to preserve fertility for the future.

On bimanual examination there is uterosacral nodularity and mild tenderness; the uterus is mobile. There is no adnexal mass. Pelvic transvaginal ultrasound shows a 2 cm endometrioma on the left ovary and no other significant findings. She has no medical comorbidity, is a non-smoker, has a body mass index of 24, and her blood pressure is normal. She has tried ibuprofen and mefenamic acid which have not been adequate.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Bimanual: uterosacral nodularity and mild tenderness, mobile uterus, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: 2 cm left ovarian endometrioma, normal uterus and right ovary; FBC haemoglobin 119 g/L (115-165), ferritin 18 micrograms/L (30-300)
data_table.Medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg as needed; mefenamic acid 500 mg three times daily; oral iron

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for diagnostic laparoscopy and definitive excision of all peritoneal endometriotic deposits
Trial GnRH agonist therapy with add-back hormone replacement for 6 months as the first hormonal option
Commence continuous combined oral contraception or a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system with NSAIDs for breakthrough pain
Refer for ovarian endometrioma cystectomy now given the 2 cm finding on transvaginal ultrasound today
Commence danazol 200 mg orally daily for 6 months with monthly clinical and biochemical monitoring

stem:
A 28-year-old woman gravida 2 para 1 presents to your tertiary delivery suite at 31 weeks plus 2 days with a confirmed gush of clear fluid 2 hours ago. She is not contracting. Her last delivery was a normal vaginal birth at term. She is well in herself. Her booking screen for group B streptococcus was negative; she has no other infection risk factors. The fetus is in cephalic presentation with reassuring antenatal records.

On sterile speculum examination, clear pooling is seen in the posterior fornix and a positive amniotic fluid test confirms ruptured membranes. The cervix appears uneffaced and closed. Maternal temperature, uterine tenderness, and fetal heart rate tracing are normal. Bedside transabdominal ultrasound shows a single fetus in cephalic position with significantly reduced amniotic fluid index but persistent fetal movements and no fetal anomalies. She has not received antenatal steroids in this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 116/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C; fetal heart rate baseline 140 bpm with reactive trace
data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum: clear pooling, no offensive odour, cervix closed; abdomen soft, non-tender, no contractions palpable
data_table.Investigations: FBC and CRP within normal limits; amniotic fluid test positive; transabdominal ultrasound single cephalic fetus, AFI reduced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management bundle?

options.text: Immediate caesarean section regardless of cervical status given the gestation and rupture of membranes today
Antenatal corticosteroids, erythromycin 10 days, magnesium sulfate if delivery within 24 hours, and expectant management with daily review
Single dose corticosteroids and immediate induction of labour with synthetic oxytocin via continuous infusion
Administer tocolysis with nifedipine for 48 hours and discharge home with twice-weekly outpatient surveillance
Commence amoxicillin and clavulanic acid orally for 10 days as antibiotic prophylaxis from time of confirmed rupture

stem:
A 32-year-old woman attends your reproductive medicine clinic after three first-trimester miscarriages over 18 months, all confirmed by ultrasound as missed miscarriages between 7 and 9 weeks gestation. She had a calf deep vein thrombosis 4 years ago after a long-haul flight, treated with 3 months of warfarin. She is currently not pregnant, has regular menstrual cycles, normal pelvic ultrasound and uterine cavity assessment, and a normal partner semen analysis.

Initial screening 6 weeks ago detected a weakly positive lupus anticoagulant by dilute Russell viper venom time on a single occasion. Anti-cardiolipin IgG and anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I antibodies were both negative. Antinuclear antibody screen was negative. Inherited thrombophilia panel was negative. Karyotype on both partners and products of conception are normal. She asks 'should I just start aspirin and heparin if I get pregnant again?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no oedema, no rash, no synovitis
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant weakly positive (dilute Russell viper venom time) on single sample 6 weeks ago; anti-cardiolipin IgG negative; anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I negative; ANA negative; inherited thrombophilia screen negative; parental karyotype normal; products of conception karyotype normal; pelvic ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence low-dose aspirin and low-molecular-weight heparin now and continue when she next becomes pregnant
Refer for in vitro fertilisation with preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy on every embryo created
Commence empirical prednisolone 10 mg daily from a positive pregnancy test for empirical immune modulation
Refer for hysteroscopy and adhesion assessment under general anaesthetic prior to any further conception attempt
Repeat the lupus anticoagulant assay 12 weeks after the initial positive sample before any treatment decision

stem:
A 28-year-old primigravida at 34+4 weeks gestation is admitted to your delivery suite with a 1-day history of frontal headache and right upper quadrant pain. Her midwife says 'her blood pressure has been creeping up and the protein-creatinine ratio came back high'. She has had three booking visits with normal blood pressure and a normal 20-week morphology scan. She has no history of seizures and no chronic hypertension.

On examination she is alert, GCS 15, with normal cranial nerves. Reflexes are brisk symmetrically with 2 beats of clonus at both ankles. Abdomen is gravid with mild right upper quadrant tenderness and a single live fetus on cardiotocography with a reassuring trace. Her vital signs include BP 168/112 mmHg confirmed on repeat manual reading 15 minutes apart.
