Bloods show platelets 122 x10^9/L (150-450), ALT 96 U/L (under 35), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.16-0.36), and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 78 mg/mmol (under 30).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 168/112 mmHg confirmed on repeat manual reading, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 142 bpm reassuring
data_table.Examination: Alert, GCS 15, brisk reflexes with 2 beats clonus bilaterally, RUQ tenderness, gravid abdomen, single fetus on CTG
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 122 x10^9/L (150-450), ALT 96 U/L (under 35), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.16-0.36), urine PCR 78 mg/mmol (under 30)
data_table.Medications: Nil regular antenatally; intravenous labetalol bolus 20 mg given prior to your review

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate loading 4 g over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour as eclampsia prophylaxis
Add oral nifedipine immediate release for ongoing blood pressure control without seizure prophylaxis cover
Commence intravenous phenytoin loading dose for seizure prophylaxis instead of magnesium sulfate
Hold further therapy pending repeat blood pressure in 30 minutes and bedside ultrasound for fetal wellbeing
Administer intramuscular betamethasone alone for fetal lung maturation and arrange transfer to tertiary unit

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P3 has just had a normal vaginal birth at 39+5 weeks gestation. The placenta delivered intact 12 minutes ago and the midwife says 'the uterus feels boggy and there's a steady fresh red trickle of blood'. Estimated blood loss is now 800 mL and continuing. Active management of the third stage was used with intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU.

On examination her airway is patent, she is talking but slightly anxious, and her conjunctivae are pink. The fundus is palpable above the umbilicus and not contracted. The vulva and lower vagina are inspected and there are no genital tract lacerations needing suture; the placenta is intact when re-examined. Bedside coagulation testing has been sent and is pending. Bimanual uterine massage has been initiated and the bladder has been emptied with a urinary catheter that has just been inserted. Intravenous access is established with a 16 G cannula running 0.9% sodium chloride.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 regular, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Boggy poorly contracted uterus above the umbilicus, no perineal laceration, placenta inspected and intact, fresh red ongoing trickle, catheter inserted, 16 G IV access
data_table.Investigations: FBC, coags, fibrinogen, group and hold sent; bedside lactate 2.1 mmol/L (under 2.0)
data_table.Medications: Active third stage included intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Administer intravenous oxytocin 5 IU slowly then commence an oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1000 mL over 4 hours
Inject intramuscular ergometrine 250 mcg without prior assessment of blood pressure or pre-eclampsia history
Administer rectal misoprostol 800 mcg as the only uterotonic without intravenous oxytocin or massage
Proceed directly to balloon tamponade with a Bakri balloon as the first step in pharmacological management
Withhold further uterotonics and observe for spontaneous uterine contraction over the next 15 minutes

stem:
A 22-year-old woman attends your general practice clinic for advice about missed combined oral contraceptive pills. She says 'I forgot two active pills in a row, the ones in the second week of the packet, and we had sex 24 hours after the second missed pill without protection'. She has been on the same monophasic 30 microgram ethinylestradiol pill for 18 months with no breakthrough bleeding. Her last menstrual period started on day 1 of her current packet 9 days ago.

She has no recent illness, no diarrhoea or vomiting, and is not taking any enzyme-inducing medication. She has not had unprotected sex earlier in the cycle. She wishes to continue the pill but is anxious about pregnancy risk. She has no past history of venous thromboembolism, migraine with aura, or breast cancer. Her BMI is 24 kg/m squared. She asks whether she needs emergency contraception now, when to start her next packet, and how to handle the rest of this packet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Well, no abdominal tenderness, no breast lump on screening
data_table.Investigations: Urinary pregnancy test today negative
data_table.Medications: Monophasic combined oral contraceptive 30 mcg ethinylestradiol; no enzyme inducers

lead_in: What is the single best management plan?

options.text: Take the most recent missed pill, continue the rest of the packet, and omit the inactive pills at packet end
Take the most recent missed pill, finish the current packet, and use condoms for the next 7 days as backup
Stop the current pill packet immediately, give emergency contraception now, and restart pills next cycle
Provide ulipristal acetate emergency contraception, continue current pills, and use condoms for 5 days
Take both missed pills together with the next scheduled pill and continue the inactive pills as planned

subtopic_detail: Gestational diabetes diagnosis and insulin initiation
stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 at 28+2 weeks gestation attends your antenatal clinic for review of her oral glucose tolerance test results. She is asymptomatic. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated with a baby weighing 3.4 kg born at term. Her BMI is 30 kg/m squared and she has no personal history of impaired glucose tolerance.

Her 75 g OGTT results are: fasting venous plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L (under 5.1), 1-hour 11.4 mmol/L (under 10.0), 2-hour 8.9 mmol/L (under 8.5). Antenatal blood pressure has been normal. The 28-week scan shows estimated fetal weight on the 60th centile, normal amniotic fluid index, and normal umbilical artery Dopplers. She has commenced ADIPS-style structured education with the diabetes educator and lifestyle measures for 2 weeks. A home glucose diary shows fasting glucose values consistently 5.6 to 5.9 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial values 8.2 to 9.4 mmol/L, despite good adherence to dietary advice.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 148 bpm
data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height 28 cm, no oedema, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT fasting 5.4 mmol/L (under 5.1), 1-hour 11.4 mmol/L (under 10.0), 2-hour 8.9 mmol/L (under 8.5); home glucose diary fasting 5.6-5.9 and postprandial 8.2-9.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lifestyle measures alone for a further 2 weeks before any consideration of pharmacological treatment
Commence subcutaneous insulin therapy with isophane (NPH) at night and short-acting insulin with main meals
Commence empirical glibenclamide as oral hypoglycaemic monotherapy without a discussion of insulin alternative
Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test in 4 weeks to confirm gestational diabetes before any treatment escalation
Plan induction of labour at 37+0 weeks irrespective of current glycaemic control or fetal growth trajectory

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P2 at 30+5 weeks gestation is brought by ambulance with a 2-hour history of painless bright red fresh vaginal bleeding. She says 'I noticed a gush of blood when I went to the toilet, no warning, no pain'. Estimated blood loss at home was about 200 mL and continues as a steady trickle. She has had two previous lower-segment caesarean births.

On examination she is anxious but talking, with no abdominal pain or tenderness. The uterus is soft and non-irritable. Speculum examination has NOT been performed yet. Fetal heart rate is reassuring with no decelerations on cardiotocography. Her 20-week morphology scan reported a posterior placenta with the lower edge 8 mm from the internal os. A repeat scan at 28 weeks confirmed placental edge covering the internal os (Grade 4 placenta praevia) with hyperechoic placental lacunae and loss of clear zone, raising suspicion of placenta accreta spectrum.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 regular, BP 108/64 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal HR 142 bpm reassuring on CTG
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender non-irritable uterus, fresh ongoing trickle visible at vulva, no speculum or digital examination performed
data_table.Investigations: FBC, coags, fibrinogen, group and screen sent; bedside Hb 108 g/L; 28-week scan: placenta covering os (Grade 4 praevia) with lacunae and loss of clear zone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix and the cause of the antepartum haemorrhage
Admit, secure two large-bore IV cannulae, administer antenatal corticosteroids, and arrange tertiary transfer
Proceed immediately to emergency caesarean delivery under general anaesthetic regardless of maternal stability
Discharge home after bleeding settles with strict bed rest, daily kick chart, and review in 1 week clinic
Commence intramuscular ergometrine 250 mcg for uterine tone in suspected placental abruption with bleeding

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 at 37+0 weeks gestation with a dichorionic diamniotic (DCDA) twin pregnancy attends your antenatal clinic for delivery planning. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Both fetuses are cephalic on this morning's growth scan, with concordant estimated fetal weights (twin 1 estimated 2.8 kg, twin 2 estimated 2.7 kg, both above the 10th centile). Amniotic fluid volumes are normal in both sacs and umbilical artery Dopplers are normal.

She has no prior caesarean and her previous singleton birth was a spontaneous vaginal delivery at term. Maternal blood pressure has been normal throughout. There is no diabetes, no cholestasis, and no growth restriction. The booking ultrasound at 11+3 weeks documented dichorionic diamniotic placentation with a lambda sign. She is keen for vaginal birth if safe and asks about timing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, twin 1 HR 138 bpm, twin 2 HR 144 bpm
data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height 40 cm, both twins cephalic on scan, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: Growth scan today: twin 1 EFW 2.8 kg (>10th), twin 2 EFW 2.7 kg (>10th), normal AFI and umbilical Dopplers both

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for timing of birth?

options.text: Plan elective caesarean delivery at 36+0 weeks gestation regardless of presentation of the twins
Recommend planned birth at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks gestation by mode appropriate to fetal presentation at the time
Defer until 40+0 weeks gestation provided cardiotocography, growth, and Dopplers remain normal weekly
Plan elective caesarean delivery at 38+0 weeks gestation because both twins are cephalic and concordant
Plan vaginal birth at 39+0 to 40+0 weeks regardless of presentations because the pregnancy has been uneventful

subtopic_detail: Adnexal mass risk of malignancy assessment
stem:
A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman attends your general gynaecology clinic with 6 weeks of vague bloating and early satiety. She says 'my pants feel tight at the waistband, my appetite is off, and food sits in me for ages'. There is no abnormal vaginal bleeding, no haematuria, and no abdominal pain. Her mother and maternal aunt had breast cancer; she does not know whether either had ovarian cancer. She had a normal age-appropriate Cervical Screening Test 1 year ago.

On examination her abdomen is mildly distended without ascites detectable clinically. Bimanual examination palpates a non-tender right adnexal mass approximately 10 cm in diameter. Pelvic ultrasound performed by the radiology department reports a 9 by 8 by 7 cm right ovarian mass with multilocular solid components, papillary projections more than 7 mm, no acoustic shadowing, and Doppler colour score 4 (very strong vascularity); ascites volume mild. Serum CA-125 is 480 kU/L (under 35) and HE4 is markedly raised. ROMA score is in the high-risk range.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mildly distended abdomen, mild shifting dullness equivocal, non-tender right adnexal mass approximately 10 cm bimanually
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: 9x8x7 cm right ovarian multilocular solid mass with papillary projections >7 mm, Doppler colour score 4, mild ascites; CA-125 480 kU/L (under 35); HE4 raised; ROMA high-risk; FBC and UEC within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to a gynaecological oncologist for staging laparotomy and intraoperative tumour assessment
Arrange image-guided percutaneous biopsy of the ovarian mass before any operative management discussion
Trial 3 months of cyclical combined oral contraceptive therapy to assess for functional cyst regression
Repeat pelvic ultrasound and CA-125 measurement in 6 weeks before referring for any specialist opinion
Commence empirical letrozole therapy for presumed oestrogen-driven ovarian neoplasm before surgical evaluation

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a regional referral hospital. You are called to a labour room at 3 am for a 26-year-old G2P1 at 36+4 weeks gestation. She has spontaneous rupture of membranes 5 minutes ago. The midwife says 'when her waters broke I could see a loop of cord at the introitus, and the heart rate has dropped'. The baby was breech on the morning scan and she had been awaiting external cephalic version this week.

On examination the cord is visible and pulsatile at the introitus. The presenting part is high and not engaged. Cardiotocography shows a sustained fetal bradycardia at 70 bpm without recovery for the past 3 minutes. The cervix is 5 cm dilated. The mother has no epidural in situ and has had no recent oral intake. Theatre is on the same floor and immediately accessible; anaesthetic and paediatric teams have been activated. She is haemodynamically stable. There is no PPH and no bleeding. The cord pH from a small sample is not available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal HR sustained 70 bpm on CTG
data_table.Examination: Pulsatile cord visible at introitus, presenting part high, breech presentation, cervix 5 cm dilated, no PPH
data_table.Investigations: Fetal heart trace shows sustained bradycardia; no cord pH available; cross-match pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate single best action?

options.text: Manually elevate the presenting part to relieve cord compression and proceed to emergency caesarean delivery now
Attempt manual cord reduction back through the cervix into the uterus and proceed with vaginal breech delivery
Wrap the prolapsed cord in warmed saline gauze, attempt vaginal examination repeatedly, and observe in delivery suite
Commence intravenous terbutaline as tocolysis and arrange routine category 2 caesarean within 75 minutes
Wait 5 minutes for spontaneous heart rate recovery before deciding between vaginal breech and operative delivery

stem:
A 27-year-old G2P1 at 39+2 weeks gestation is in your delivery suite in active second stage of labour with vertex presentation. The midwife performs a vaginal examination after a sudden gush of fluid and calls you saying 'there's a pulsating loop of cord palpable past the vertex and the fetal heart rate has dropped'. The cervix is fully dilated and the head is at station plus 1.

On examination she is alert and lying on her back. She has had an uncomplicated antenatal course apart from gestational hypertension controlled on labetalol. Her last vaginal examination 30 minutes ago showed full dilatation and station plus 1. The CTG had been reactive prior to the current event. The on-call obstetric consultant and anaesthetist are 3 minutes away. The theatre is empty and ready for a category 1 caesarean if needed. The bladder is empty. Her epidural is functioning well with adequate sensory block to the umbilicus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 134/82 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 70 bpm sustained
data_table.Examination: Cervix fully dilated, head at station plus 1, pulsating cord palpable past the vertex, intact membranes ruptured
data_table.Investigations: CTG previously reactive, now sustained bradycardia fetal HR 70 bpm
data_table.Medications: Epidural with adequate block to umbilicus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Place the mother in steep Trendelenburg position and arrange transfer to theatre for category 1 caesarean section
Manually elevate the presenting part with a gloved hand and fill the bladder with 500-700 mL of saline
Proceed to immediate instrumental vaginal birth with vacuum or forceps assistance in the delivery room now
Push the cord back above the presenting part and continue active second stage with directed pushing efforts
Administer intravenous terbutaline 250 microgram tocolysis and arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging

stem:
A 31-year-old G1P0 is referred to your fetal medicine clinic at 29+3 weeks gestation for severe early-onset fetal growth restriction. She has had one prior morphology scan at 20 weeks (normal) and a growth scan at 28 weeks showed estimated fetal weight at the 2nd centile. She has had no antepartum haemorrhage and no abdominal pain. Her booking visit blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg.

The current scan today shows estimated fetal weight 850 g (under 3rd centile), abdominal circumference under 3rd centile, head circumference at the 25th centile, amniotic fluid index 4 cm (deepest pool 2 cm), umbilical artery Doppler with absent end-diastolic flow, middle cerebral artery pulsatility index 0.78 (under 5th centile for gestation), and ductus venosus a-wave absent. She has had a normal full antenatal screen for infection and a normal karyotype. CTG shows reduced short-term variability over a 60-minute computerised assessment. Her blood pressure is 142/92 mmHg today and a spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 36 mg/mmol.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 142/92 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 142 bpm
data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 24 cm, soft abdomen, no tenderness
data_table.Investigations: EFW 850 g under 3rd centile; AC under 3rd centile; AFI 4 cm; UA Doppler absent end-diastolic flow; MCA PI 0.78; ductus venosus a-wave absent; computerised CTG reduced STV; urine PCR 36 mg/mmol
data_table.Medications: Two doses intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg given 24 and 12 hours ago; intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion started 4 hours ago for neuroprotection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue inpatient observation with twice-daily computerised CTG and Doppler in 1 week for ongoing monitoring
Wait until 30 weeks completed gestation before commencing any plan for delivery for additional fetal maturity
Proceed to category 2 caesarean section once magnesium sulfate neuroprotection is complete with neonatal team in attendance
Induce labour with oral mifepristone followed by a vaginal prostaglandin pessary and aim for vaginal birth
Treat the maternal blood pressure with labetalol and reassess fetal status after 48 hours of antihypertensive control

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in delivery suite. A 34-year-old G3P3 has just delivered a 4.1 kg baby vaginally. Active management of the third stage was given. The midwife was applying cord traction when there was a sudden gush of blood and the mother became pale and clammy. The midwife says 'the fundus has disappeared and I can feel something like a bag at the introitus'.

On examination she is conscious but pale and diaphoretic. There is a large dark red mass visible at the introitus. The uterine fundus is no longer palpable abdominally. Estimated blood loss is now 1500 mL and increasing. She is in significant pain. Intravenous access has been established with a 16 G cannula and 0.9% sodium chloride is running. The anaesthetic registrar is in the room. The placenta is not yet delivered and appears still attached to the inverted uterine fundus. Bedside coagulation is pending. Bedside lactate is 3.6 mmol/L (under 2.0).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 thready, BP 78/42 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99% on 6 L/min mask oxygen, temperature 36.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Conscious pale diaphoretic, large dark red mass at the introitus, no fundus palpable abdominally, placenta still attached to inverted fundus
data_table.Investigations: FBC and coags sent, bedside lactate 3.6 mmol/L (under 2.0)
data_table.Medications: Active third stage included intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU; 0.9% sodium chloride running through 16 G cannula

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Cease all uterotonics, leave the placenta attached, and immediately attempt manual replacement of the inverted fundus
Remove the placenta manually first to reduce blood loss, then attempt replacement of the inverted fundus
Commence intravenous ergometrine 250 microgram before any attempt at manual reduction of the uterine fundus
Immediately transfer to theatre for emergency abdominal hysterectomy under general anaesthesia as the first step
Apply firm bimanual compression with two hands and administer intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram immediately

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P1 at 37+0 weeks gestation is on your delivery suite for a planned induction. She had a velamentous cord insertion identified at her 20-week morphology scan with vasa praevia confirmed on transvaginal scan at 32 weeks. Antenatal corticosteroids were given at 32 and 34 weeks, and she has been admitted as an inpatient since 34 weeks for monitoring.

A few minutes after artificial rupture of membranes by the registrar (at 4 cm cervical dilation), the midwife reports a small painless gush of bright red blood. CTG immediately shows a sinusoidal trace with reduced variability and a baseline of 130 bpm. The previously reactive trace before ARM had a baseline of 140 bpm with moderate variability. Maternal observations remain stable. Theatre is staffed and the anaesthetic team is already in the room. Her booking blood group is O positive with no antibodies. She has had no prior caesarean and her epidural is functioning.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal HR 130 bpm sinusoidal
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, membranes ruptured, small bright red painless gush ongoing, fetal head at station 0
data_table.Investigations: CTG sinusoidal trace; Kleihauer test sent; FBC, group and hold available
data_table.Medications: Two doses antenatal betamethasone 11.4 mg at 32 and 34 weeks; functioning epidural

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Continue induction of labour and aim for vaginal birth with continuous CTG monitoring and operative delivery if needed
Administer maternal intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g and arrange fetal blood transfusion in the neonatal unit
Perform manual digital tamponade against the bleeding vessel and observe CTG for spontaneous recovery over 15 minutes
Activate the category 1 caesarean section pathway with delivery within 30 minutes and neonatal team in attendance
Send urgent Kleihauer test and Apt test for fetal blood differentiation before deciding mode of delivery

stem:
A 29-year-old G1P1 woman is brought to your emergency department day 4 after a normal vaginal birth at term. Her partner says 'she's been getting more confused all day, her tummy is rock hard and she's gone really cold and shaky'. She had a brief sore throat the day before delivery. There is no history of antenatal infection and her group B streptococcus screen was negative.

On examination she is drowsy (GCS 13), with cool peripheries and mottled lower limbs. She has marked uterine tenderness, foul-smelling pinkish lochia, and a rigid abdomen. There is no breast erythema. Bedside lactate is 5.8 mmol/L (under 2.0); white cell count is 28 x10^9/L (4-11) with 92% neutrophils; CRP is 320 mg/L (under 5); creatinine has risen from 60 to 132 micromol/L. Bedside ultrasound shows retained products of conception 32 mm. She is exclusively breastfeeding a healthy term baby. The pelvic examination reveals an open cervical os with passage of foul-smelling discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13, cool peripheries with mottled lower limbs, rigid abdomen with uterine tenderness, foul-smelling lochia, open cervical os
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 5.8 mmol/L (under 2.0), WCC 28 x10^9/L (4-11) 92% neutrophils, CRP 320 mg/L (under 5), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90), retained products of conception 32 mm on bedside ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous oral metronidazole monotherapy with intravenous fluids and observation for 6 hours
Intravenous benzylpenicillin alone with intravenous fluids and immediate transfer to the postnatal ward
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g, metronidazole 500 mg, plus clindamycin 600 mg every 8 hours and urgent surgical evacuation
Intravenous oral cefalexin and oral metronidazole pending culture results with outpatient follow-up in 48 hours
Intravenous vancomycin alone for presumed methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus puerperal mastitis

stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar at a regional hospital seeing a 33-year-old G2P1 woman at 36 weeks for a planning discussion about her mode of birth. Her previous birth was an emergency lower segment caesarean section at term two years ago for arrest of dilation at 6 cm despite syntocinon augmentation; the baby was 3.6 kg and the operation note describes a transverse lower segment incision with no extension. She has had no other pregnancies.

This pregnancy has been uncomplicated. The fetus is cephalic, estimated fetal weight on a growth scan two days ago is 3.4 kg with normal umbilical artery dopplers, and the placenta is fundal. Her body mass index at booking was 28 kg/m2. She has had no interpregnancy interval issues and is keen to attempt a vaginal birth. The regional hospital has a 24/7 obstetrician on call, an in-house anaesthetist, blood bank availability, and a 30 minute decision-to-delivery audit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 142/min
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 36 cm, longitudinal lie, cephalic, free 4/5; uterus soft and non-tender
data_table.History: G2P1; previous LSCS at term for arrest of dilation; transverse lower segment incision; current EFW 3.4 kg; BMI 28

lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling recommendation?

options.text: Advise that vaginal birth is contraindicated because of her body mass index of 28 kg/m2
Recommend elective repeat caesarean section at 39 weeks given prior arrest of dilation
Induce labour at 39 weeks with prostaglandin gel to optimise her chance of vaginal birth
Offer trial of labour after caesarean with continuous CTG and IV access from established labour
Arrange external cephalic version at 37 weeks before any further mode of birth discussion

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the assessment unit at 11pm for a 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 32+4 weeks brought in by her partner with a frontal headache for 6 hours and three episodes of vomiting. She has been seeing a midwife at a low-risk shared care clinic. Booking BP was 110/70 mmHg.

On arrival she is reactive but withdrawn. Repeat manual BP measurements over 15 minutes are 168/112, 172/108 and 165/110 mmHg. Reflexes are brisk with 3 beats of ankle clonus. There is no visual scotoma. Urine dipstick shows protein 3+. CTG shows a baseline of 145/min with normal variability and accelerations, no decelerations. The bed manager confirms a tertiary neonatal unit cot is available 90 minutes away by retrieval.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98/min, BP 168/112 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 145/min
data_table.Examination: Reactive, withdrawn; brisk reflexes with 3 beats clonus; no scotoma; no epigastric tenderness; SFH 33 cm
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick protein 3+; platelets 142 x10^9/L (150-400); ALT 78 U/L (<40); creatinine 88 micromol/L; uric acid raised; PlGF assay pending
data_table.CTG: Baseline 145/min, normal variability, accelerations present, no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous furosemide 40 mg as a single bolus for pulmonary oedema prophylaxis
Commence betamethasone 11.4 mg IM and plan delivery in the morning by elective caesarean
Oral nifedipine 20 mg immediate-release and IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose, then arrange retrieval
Discharge home on oral labetalol 100 mg three times daily with day-stay review tomorrow
Start an intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion targeting mean arterial pressure under 80 mmHg

stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar reviewing a 35-year-old G2P1 woman at 32+0 weeks gestation in the joint obstetric-endocrine clinic. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks on a 75g OGTT (fasting 5.3, 1 hour 11.2, 2 hour 9.4 mmol/L). She has been on dietary modification plus metformin 1 g twice daily for the last four weeks. She is otherwise well; her BMI at booking was 31 kg/m2 and her previous pregnancy was complicated by a 4.1 kg neonate at term without operative delivery.

Her blood glucose monitoring diary over the last 14 days shows fasting capillary glucoses ranging 5.6 to 6.1 mmol/L (target <5.1), one hour postprandial values ranging 7.5 to 8.4 mmol/L (target <7.4), and she reports good dietary adherence with a low GI breakfast. Her HbA1c last week was 5.8%. A growth ultrasound today shows estimated fetal weight on the 92nd centile with a normal abdominal circumference to head circumference ratio.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 140/min
data_table.BGL diary: Fasting 5.6 to 6.1 mmol/L (target <5.1); 1 hour postprandial 7.5 to 8.4 mmol/L (target <7.4)
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 5.8%; EFW 92nd centile; AC:HC ratio normal; amniotic fluid index 18 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add bedtime intermediate-acting insulin isophane 8 units and continue metformin
Increase metformin to 1.5 g twice daily and reassess in two weeks
Switch from metformin to glibenclamide 5 mg twice daily as an alternative oral agent
Plan elective induction of labour at 37 weeks for fetal macrosomia prophylaxis
Continue current management as her HbA1c of 5.8% indicates adequate overall control

stem:
You are the postnatal ward registrar reviewing a 36-year-old G3P3 woman who delivered 8 hours ago by emergency lower segment caesarean at 38+5 weeks for failure to progress after a 14-hour labour. The procedure was uncomplicated; estimated blood loss was 750 mL. Her booking BMI was 34 kg/m2. Her mother had an unprovoked DVT at age 55 and her sister had a pulmonary embolism on the combined oral contraceptive pill in her twenties. She is otherwise well, mobilising with assistance, and the urinary catheter has been removed.

A thrombophilia screen taken at booking by her general practitioner before this admission showed her to be heterozygous for the factor V Leiden mutation. She is not breastfeeding by choice. Today's full blood count is normal, renal function is preserved (creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR >90), and there is no active bleeding from her wound or her vagina. The midwife asks you to prescribe thromboprophylaxis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable, mobilising with assistance; dry wound; lochia normal; calves soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits; creatinine 68 micromol/L; eGFR >90 mL/min; factor V Leiden heterozygous

lead_in: What is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis prescription?

options.text: Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for 7 days only, then mechanical prophylaxis
Subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily for 6 weeks plus graduated compression stockings
Graduated compression stockings alone for 6 weeks without pharmacological prophylaxis
Aspirin 100 mg orally daily for 6 weeks for venous thromboembolism prevention
Therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily for 3 months given factor V Leiden

stem:
You are the antenatal day-assessment registrar reviewing a 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 36+6 weeks gestation who has been referred from her shared-care GP for a breech presentation noted clinically and confirmed on a presentation scan today. She had a normal vaginal birth at term with her first pregnancy two years ago.

This pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Symphysis fundal height is 36 cm, the presenting part is high, and CTG today is normal. The growth scan two weeks ago showed an estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile, amniotic fluid index 14 cm, and the placenta was reported as fundo-anterior with no praevia. Today's presentation scan confirms a frank breech with extended legs and re-states the placenta as fundo-anterior. There is no rupture of membranes, no antepartum haemorrhage and no history of previous uterine surgery. She is keen to attempt a vaginal birth and asks about turning the baby.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 142/min
data_table.Examination: SFH 36 cm; presenting part high; uterus soft and non-tender; no PV bleeding; no rupture of membranes
data_table.Investigations: Presentation scan: frank breech with extended legs; AFI 14 cm; placenta fundo-anterior; no praevia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer all action and rescan at 38 weeks to allow possible spontaneous version to occur
Recommend elective caesarean section at 39 weeks without first offering external cephalic version
Plan a trial of vaginal breech birth at term with continuous CTG monitoring as first option
Refer for moxibustion at acupuncture point BL67 daily for 14 days before any further decision
Schedule external cephalic version at 37 weeks with terbutaline tocolysis and post-procedure CTG

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the high-risk antenatal clinic reviewing a 31-year-old G3P1 woman at 14+0 weeks gestation. Her first pregnancy ended in a painless second-trimester loss at 22 weeks following spontaneous rupture of membranes preceded by silent cervical dilation; her second pregnancy ended in a similar loss at 20 weeks. Neither loss had infective features and both placentas showed no chorioamnionitis on histology. She has no other gynaecological history and her first-trimester anatomy and screening have been low risk.

A transvaginal ultrasound today shows a closed external os with a cervical length of 28 mm and no funnelling. Her current pregnancy is singleton, the fetus is structurally normal at the 12-week morphology scan, and the placenta is fundal. She has no vaginal bleeding, no abdominal pain, and no signs of preterm labour. There is no history of cervical surgery or LLETZ. She asks what can be done to reduce the chance of losing this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 158/min
data_table.Examination: Closed external os on speculum; no PV bleeding; uterus appropriate for gestation
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: cervical length 28 mm, no funnelling; singleton; structural anatomy normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intervention?

options.text: History indicated cerclage now plus daily vaginal progesterone 200 mg from 16 weeks
Serial transvaginal cervical length scans every 2 weeks and intervene only if shortening
Bed rest at home from 16 weeks until 36 weeks with avoidance of intercourse
Place an abdominal cerclage by laparoscopy at 12 weeks given two previous failures
Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM weekly from 24 weeks prophylactically

stem:
You are the on-call obstetric registrar reviewing a 26-year-old G1P0 woman in active labour at 39+4 weeks gestation. Her membranes ruptured 22 hours ago and she has had spontaneous progress to 5 cm dilation with regular contractions. She had a prolonged second stage planned and is on an epidural. Her group B streptococcus swab at 36 weeks was negative.

Over the last hour her temperature has risen from 36.9 °C to 38.4 °C, recorded by the midwife on two readings 20 minutes apart. Her maternal heart rate is 118/min. Fetal CTG shows a baseline of 168/min with reduced variability and no decelerations. The amniotic fluid drained at vaginal examination is cloudy and offensive. She is otherwise stable, with a normal blood pressure and respiratory rate, and is comfortable on epidural with no abdominal tenderness between contractions. She is not allergic to penicillin or to any other medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 122/72 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.4 °C, fetal heart 168/min baseline
data_table.Examination: 5 cm dilation; cloudy offensive amniotic fluid; no abdominal tenderness; epidural in situ
data_table.Investigations: Maternal CTG baseline 168/min reduced variability no decelerations; WCC pending; GBS swab negative at 36 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until blood cultures return and target therapy then
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 4-hourly alone for GBS coverage
Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus metronidazole 500 mg 12-hourly
Oral cefalexin 500 mg 6-hourly plus expectant management of labour
Intravenous ampicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily

stem:
You are the senior obstetric registrar at a tertiary delivery suite called urgently to a 34-year-old G4P3 woman who collapsed two minutes after the spontaneous vaginal birth of a 4.2 kg male infant at 41+2 weeks. The third stage had been managed actively with intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU. The placenta is in situ.

While you arrive she becomes unresponsive, has a witnessed seizure, and stops breathing. Pulse is impalpable centrally. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is commenced immediately. The midwife reports she became suddenly breathless, said she felt cold, and complained of impending doom moments before losing consciousness. There was a small amount of pink frothy sputum at her mouth. She has no past history of asthma or epilepsy, did not receive epidural, and a peripheral cannula sited 30 minutes ago for hydration has been kept patent. The first bloods drawn during resuscitation show a fibrinogen of 0.8 g/L (1.5-4.0), platelets 78 x10^9/L, INR 2.4 and pH 6.98.

data_table.Vital signs: No central pulse; previously: pulse 142/min, BP 70/40 mmHg, SpO2 unrecordable, RR 0 (apnoeic)
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive after seizure; pink frothy sputum at mouth; uterus tone unclear with placenta in situ; no obvious haemorrhage source
data_table.Investigations: Fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (1.5-4.0); platelets 78 x10^9/L; INR 2.4; pH 6.98; lactate 9.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer resuscitation and arrange urgent CT pulmonary angiogram to confirm pulmonary embolism
Give intravenous adrenaline 100 mcg boluses for presumed anaphylaxis to active third stage oxytocin
Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g for presumed eclampsia and continue observation
Continue CPR, secure airway, activate massive transfusion protocol, escalate to obstetric and ICU consultants
Start tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously and observe response before further escalation

stem:
A 32-year-old woman attends your general practice clinic with a 12-month history of progressively heavier periods. She reports cycles every 28 days lasting 8 days, soaks through a super tampon and a pad together every 1 to 2 hours on day 2 and 3, and has passed coin-sized clots. She is increasingly tired but works full time. She and her partner plan to conceive in around 12 months and want to avoid hormonal contraception. There is no dyspareunia, no intermenstrual or post coital bleeding, and no family history of bleeding disorder.

On examination she is comfortable; abdomen is soft and non-tender and no pelvic mass is palpable. Speculum and bimanual examination are normal. Cervical screening (HPV-based) is current and negative. Pelvic ultrasound is reported as a normal sized anteverted uterus with regular endometrial echotexture, no submucosal fibroid, no adenomyosis features and normal ovaries. Full blood count shows haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-160), MCV 72 fL (80-95), ferritin 8 mcg/L (30-150). Coagulation profile and von Willebrand panel are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, non-tender, no pelvic mass; speculum and bimanual normal; cervical screening current negative
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic US: normal uterus, no fibroid, no adenomyosis, normal ovaries; Hb 104 g/L, MCV 72 fL, ferritin 8 mcg/L; coagulation and von Willebrand panel within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol 30 mcg and levonorgestrel 150 mcg
Endometrial ablation under outpatient hysteroscopy after diagnostic curettage at the same sitting
GnRH agonist depot injection monthly for 6 months with low dose oestrogen add-back
Tranexamic acid 1 g orally three times daily for the first 4 days of each menstrual cycle
Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system inserted at the next available appointment

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P1 woman is referred to your gynaecology clinic with 9 months of secondary amenorrhoea. Her cycle had previously been regular every 28 days. She had a normal vaginal delivery 14 months ago, complicated by retained products of conception that required ultrasound-guided suction curettage at 6 weeks postpartum after antibiotic treatment for endometritis. She has had cyclical pelvic pain in the lower abdomen each month for the last 6 months without any associated bleeding. She is not breastfeeding.

On examination she is healthy and well. Body mass index 24 kg/m2. Abdomen is soft. Speculum examination reveals a clean cervix; bimanual examination is unremarkable. Beta-hCG is negative. Serum TSH, prolactin, FSH, LH, oestradiol and androgen panel are within the normal range. A progesterone withdrawal challenge with medroxyprogesterone 10 mg daily for 10 days produced no bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a thin discontinuous endometrium with focal anechoic areas suggesting adhesions; a saline infusion sonohysterogram shows fibrous bands crossing the uterine cavity.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Healthy, BMI 24; abdomen soft; speculum and bimanual unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative; TSH, prolactin, FSH, LH, oestradiol and androgens within normal limits; progesterone withdrawal: no bleed; TV US: thin discontinuous endometrium; saline sonohysterogram: intrauterine adhesions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with chromopertubation to exclude tubal disease before any treatment
Repeat dilation and curettage to clear suspected retained tissue with antibiotic cover
Empirical GnRH agonist therapy for 3 months and reassess endometrial pattern by ultrasound
Combined oral contraceptive pill for 6 months and reassess menstrual return after cessation
Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis under direct vision with post operative oestrogen for 8 weeks

stem:
A 29-year-old nulliparous woman presents to your general practice for the third time in 9 months distressed by severe irritability, low mood, anxiety, breast tenderness and bloating that begin around 7 days before menses and resolve fully within 2 days of menses starting. She has used the eCOPE prospective symptom diary for 3 consecutive cycles which shows at least 5 symptoms in the luteal phase with full resolution in the follicular phase and no symptoms outside the luteal phase.

On examination she is well, with a normal mood when reviewed in the follicular phase today. PHQ-9 outside the luteal phase is 2 of 27 and GAD-7 is 1 of 21; both rise sharply in the luteal phase. She has tried regular exercise and dietary change for 4 months without benefit. There is no history of bipolar affective disorder, no current alcohol or recreational drug use, no concomitant medications and no contraception is in use because she and her partner are happy with condoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Well, mood reactive; eCOPE diary: at least 5 luteal symptoms, full follicular resolution across 3 cycles
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 follicular 2/27 (rises sharply in luteal phase); GAD-7 follicular 1/21; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily commenced 14 days before expected menses each cycle
Lithium carbonate 600 mg taken nightly with monthly serum lithium concentration monitoring
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g infusion during severe luteal flares in the day clinic
Lamotrigine titrated over 6 weeks to 100 mg daily with rash monitoring during build up
Combined oral contraceptive pill containing drospirenone taken cyclically with a 4 day break

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P2 woman presents to your general practice at 6 weeks postpartum for her routine review. She has had two uncomplicated vaginal deliveries; the youngest is exclusively breastfed and feeding 3 to 4 hourly day and night. Her previous postnatal contraception was a progesterone only pill that she found unreliable and she has a 12 year history of menorrhagia previously controlled on combined oral contraceptive pill. She and her partner have completed their family but are not yet committed to permanent sterilisation. She has had no bleeding for the last 7 days and there has been no resumption of menses.

On examination she is well. Body mass index is 25 kg/m2. Blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg. Speculum examination shows a clean cervix and bimanual examination reveals a normally involuted uterus, no adnexal tenderness and no mass. A urine pregnancy test in the consulting room is negative. There is no current pelvic infection and she has had no STI risk in the last 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Well, BMI 25; speculum clean cervix; bimanual: involuted uterus, no adnexal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative; no current STI symptoms; no high-risk sexual contact in last 6 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive recommendation today?

options.text: Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill starting today and continuing without breaks
Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system in the same consultation today
Insert a copper intrauterine device at 12 weeks postpartum after a repeat speculum examination
Defer all contraception until resumption of menses then start the progesterone only pill
Administer depot medroxyprogesterone 150 mg intramuscular injection today and repeat every 12 weeks

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the high dependency obstetric area for a 36-year-old G2P1 woman at 35+2 weeks being managed for severe pre-eclampsia. Two hours ago she had a 4 g intravenous magnesium sulfate loading dose followed by a 1 g/hour maintenance infusion. Her blood pressure is now controlled on a labetalol infusion. She has had no seizure and the cardiotocograph remains reassuring.

The bedside midwife calls you because over the last 30 minutes the patient has become progressively drowsy, slurring her speech. Patellar reflexes are now absent bilaterally. Respiratory rate has fallen to 9 breaths per minute and she is not coughing on suctioning. Hourly urine output has dropped from 60 mL/hour to 15 mL/hour over the last 2 hours. The renal team reports her serum creatinine has risen from 78 to 156 micromol/L since admission. The point-of-care magnesium concentration just back from the laboratory is 4.5 mmol/L (therapeutic 2 to 3.5 mmol/L).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 9/min, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 140/min
data_table.Examination: Drowsy with slurred speech; patellar reflexes absent; not coughing on suctioning; urine output 15 mL/hour
data_table.Investigations: Magnesium 4.5 mmol/L (therapeutic 2-3.5); creatinine 156 micromol/L (was 78); CTG: baseline 140/min, normal variability, no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous naloxone 400 mcg titrated for respiratory depression and reassess every 5 minutes
Intubate immediately and ventilate at FiO2 100% until magnesium clearance restores breathing
Cease the magnesium infusion and administer intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 3 minutes
Switch antihypertensive control to oral nifedipine 20 mg and continue the magnesium infusion
Intravenous furosemide 40 mg to accelerate magnesium clearance and a fluid bolus of 250 mL saline

stem:
A 33-year-old G1P0 woman presents to the early pregnancy assessment service at 7 weeks gestation after a fresh embryo transfer through her local IVF clinic. She has had right iliac fossa pain over the last 24 hours, described as constant and rated 4 of 10. There has been a small amount of pink spotting today. There is no shoulder tip pain, no syncope and no significant per vaginal bleeding.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable. Abdomen is soft with mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no rebound and no guarding. Speculum examination shows a closed cervix with a small amount of fresh blood. Bimanual examination reveals fullness in the right adnexa. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine gestational sac at 7 weeks with a fetal pole, crown rump length 10 mm and fetal cardiac activity present; a separate 3 cm complex right adnexal mass adjacent to the right ovary and a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum beta-hCG is 14,200 IU/L; haemoglobin 124 g/L; her blood group is A positive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism; speculum closed cervix small fresh blood; bimanual right adnexal fullness
data_table.Investigations: TV US: viable 7-week intrauterine pregnancy with fetal cardiac activity; 3 cm complex right adnexal mass; small POD fluid; beta-hCG 14,200 IU/L; Hb 124 g/L; group A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Suction curettage of the uterine cavity followed by methotrexate for the adnexal pregnancy
Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with weekly beta-hCG monitoring thereafter
Expectant management with serial beta-hCG and ultrasound surveillance over the next 7 days
Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected tube while preserving the intrauterine pregnancy
Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU and discharge with early pregnancy unit review in 48 hours

stem:
A 35-year-old woman is referred to your colposcopy clinic with a positive cervical screening result. Eighteen months ago she had a large loop excision of the transformation zone for histologically confirmed HSIL (CIN 3) with clear excision margins of 4 mm. She had a routine test of cure cervical screening at 12 months which was reported as HPV oncogenic types not detected and she was advised to return to the routine 5 yearly screening cycle. She presented for an opportunistic test 6 months early following a recent change of general practitioner.

The current result reports HPV oncogenic type 16 detected, with reflex liquid based cytology showing HSIL. She is asymptomatic, with no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and no abnormal discharge. She is in a stable monogamous relationship and uses condoms intermittently. Her general health is good and her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. On examination the cervix appears macroscopically healthy with no visible lesion; bimanual is unremarkable. Pelvic ultrasound has been arranged but is not yet completed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Cervix macroscopically healthy with no visible lesion; bimanual unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: HPV oncogenic type 16 detected; reflex cytology HSIL; prior LLETZ for CIN 3 with 4 mm clear margins; 12-month test of cure HPV not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to total abdominal hysterectomy without prior colposcopy or histology confirmation
Repeat HPV based cervical screening in 12 months without colposcopy or biopsy intervention
Order pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to stage suspected invasive cervical malignancy first
Repeat cone biopsy by cold knife conisation in the operating theatre under regional anaesthesia
Colposcopy with directed biopsy and consideration of repeat excisional treatment if confirmed

stem:
A 22-year-old G1P0 woman had suction evacuation 4 weeks ago for a complete hydatidiform molar pregnancy diagnosed at 9 weeks gestation by uterine size larger than dates, theca lutein cysts, and 'snowstorm' ultrasound. Histology confirmed a complete mole with no evidence of invasive trophoblast on initial review. She is being followed in the Australian gestational trophoblastic registry through your tertiary unit.

Her pre-evacuation beta-hCG was 250,000 IU/L. Weekly serial concentrations have been 18,000 on day 7, 12,000 on day 14, 13,000 on day 21 and 14,000 today on day 28. She is otherwise well, with no abdominal pain, no abnormal bleeding and no respiratory or neurological symptoms. Her chest radiograph is clear without nodules. Pelvic ultrasound today shows a normally involuted uterus, no residual molar tissue and normal adnexae. Liver and renal function are within normal limits. She and her partner use barrier contraception.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Well; uterus involuted; no abnormal bleeding; chest clear; no neurological deficits
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG day 7: 18,000; day 14: 12,000; day 21: 13,000; day 28: 14,000 IU/L; CXR clear; pelvic US no residual molar tissue; LFTs and renal within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Single agent methotrexate chemotherapy 50 mg intramuscular on day 1, 3, 5, 7 every 2 weeks
Combination chemotherapy with EMA-CO protocol (etoposide, methotrexate, dactinomycin, vincristine)
Repeat suction curettage of the uterine cavity for presumed retained molar tissue under anaesthesia
Continue weekly beta-hCG monitoring without any intervention until 6 months post evacuation
Total abdominal hysterectomy with preservation of both ovaries as the definitive treatment

subtopic_detail: Atonic PPH second-line uterotonic with TXA
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a tertiary maternity unit reviewing a G3P3 woman who had a spontaneous vaginal delivery 30 minutes ago. The placenta delivered intact. The midwife now reports a steady fresh trickle and an estimated blood loss of 1500 mL over the last 10 minutes. She has had 10 units IM oxytocin at delivery and bimanual uterine compression has been commenced. There is no perineal laceration above first degree.

On assessment she is alert and oriented but cool peripherally. Her fundus is at the umbilicus and boggy on palpation. She has no history of hypertension and no asthma. She has 2 large bore cannulae and a group and hold has been sent with crossmatch in progress. The anaesthetics registrar is on the way.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 100/65 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert; cool peripheries; fundus at umbilicus, boggy; ongoing fresh PV bleeding; perineum first degree tear, sutured
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 1500 mL; Hb on antenatal bloods 118 g/L (115-160); coags and lactate sent

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next uterotonic and adjunct?

options.text: IM ergometrine 250 mcg plus IV tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes
IM carboprost 250 mcg repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses
Misoprostol 800 mcg per rectum as the sole second-line agent
Insert Bakri balloon tamponade now without further pharmacological therapy
Continue uterine massage and further IV oxytocin infusion as sole therapy

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia BP control and magnesium
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on call. A G1 primigravida at 32+4 weeks is referred from a regional hospital with severe pre-eclampsia. She reports an occipital headache and blurred vision for the past hour. She has no past medical history and was on no medications. The retrieval team is en route to transfer her to a tertiary centre with neonatal intensive care 90 minutes away.

On arrival in your obstetric unit she is alert and orientated but uncomfortable. Reflexes are brisk with no clonus. Fetal heart rate trace is reactive at 145/min with no decelerations. The midwife has just established a peripheral cannula and your consultant is on the way. Steroids for fetal lung maturity have been given by the referring hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 168/115 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal HR 145/min
data_table.Examination: Alert, uncomfortable; reflexes brisk no clonus; epigastric tenderness; lower limb oedema 2+
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 95 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 88 U/L (5-35), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urine PCR 800 mg/mmol, urate 0.42 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management bundle?

options.text: IV nifedipine 10 mg bolus plus IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose
IV labetalol 20 mg plus IV magnesium 4 g loading then 1 g/hour, target BP <160/110
IV hydralazine 10 mg every 20 minutes plus dexamethasone 12 mg for fetal maturity
Continuous IV nicardipine infusion and immediate category 1 caesarean section
Low-dose aspirin 150 mg orally plus magnesium 6 g IV loading dose only

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia escalation after McRoberts and suprapubic pressure
stem:
You are the senior O and G registrar attending an emergency call from the labour ward. A G2P1 woman at 38+0 weeks has just delivered the fetal head spontaneously after a 2 hour second stage with epidural anaesthesia. The head is turtling against the perineum and the shoulders have not delivered with the next contraction. The estimated fetal weight on the 36 week growth scan was 4100 g.

The team has applied McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal hips and suprapubic pressure (Rubin I) for the past 30 seconds without delivery. The midwife is timing each manoeuvre and the obstetric consultant has been paged and is 4 minutes away. The mother is calm with epidural anaesthesia.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 95/min, BP 122/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, fetal HR last recorded 140/min before head delivery
data_table.Examination: Fetal head delivered, turtling sign present; shoulders not delivered; perineum intact apart from small first-degree graze; bladder catheterised
data_table.Investigations: Estimated fetal weight 4100 g at 36 weeks; no GDM; previous baby 3650 g; current head-to-body delivery interval 60 seconds

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Continue McRoberts and suprapubic pressure for another 60 seconds before escalating
Zavanelli (cephalic replacement) and prepare theatre for category 1 caesarean
Internal rotation manoeuvre (Rubin II or Wood's screw) or delivery of the posterior arm
Symphysiotomy under local anaesthesia at the bedside before any further manoeuvre
Deliberate clavicle fracture by direct suprasternal pressure as next manoeuvre

subtopic_detail: Cord prolapse in regional setting with delayed transfer
stem:
You are the sole obstetric medical officer at a small regional hospital without on-site theatre or operative obstetric capability. A G2P1 woman at 37+5 weeks with a breech presentation presents with spontaneous rupture of membranes 20 minutes ago and has just been transferred from triage. On vaginal examination you palpate a pulsating umbilical cord below the presenting part. Cervix is 4 cm dilated.

The nearest tertiary maternity unit with theatre is 90 minutes away by ambulance. The retrieval team is being mobilised. The midwife is supporting the woman in left lateral position. Fetal heart rate by intermittent auscultation is 130/min with no decelerations heard so far. The mother is calm and oriented, in mild discomfort. You have IV access established.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 92/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 130/min by Pinard
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, breech presentation, pulsating cord palpable below presenting part
data_table.Investigations: Fetal HR 130/min reassuring; bedside ultrasound confirms ongoing cardiac activity

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management before retrieval?

options.text: Vertical transfer with continuous digital elevation of the presenting part throughout
Manually replace the cord into the uterus and observe with continuous CTG monitoring
Allow labour to proceed expectantly at 4 cm cervical dilatation given breech presentation
Knee-chest, retrograde bladder fill 500-700 mL warm saline via Foley, urgent caesarean
Augment with IV oxytocin infusion to expedite vaginal delivery despite cord prolapse

subtopic_detail: Maternal cardiac arrest perimortem caesarean timing
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a tertiary ED resus when a 32-year-old G1 at 28+2 weeks gestation collapses suddenly at 11:02 with witnessed cardiac arrest. CPR is commenced immediately with continuous chest compressions, manual left uterine displacement, bag-mask ventilation, and intravenous adrenaline 1 mg every 3 to 4 minutes. By 11:05 she has had three cycles of ACLS without return of spontaneous circulation.

A brief bedside ultrasound earlier in the day showed a normal fetal heart rate of 145/min at 28+2 weeks. The fundus is palpable above the umbilicus. The ED consultant is performing the airway and the anaesthetist has arrived. A surgical pack is in the resus bay. The team confirms ongoing high-quality CPR and pulselessness.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulseless, no organised rhythm; ETCO2 18 mmHg during chest compressions; fetal HR not yet rechecked since arrest
data_table.Examination: Pulseless on continuous CPR; fundus 2 cm above umbilicus; no obvious bleeding; left uterine displacement maintained
data_table.Investigations: Earlier same-day ultrasound fetal HR 145/min; rhythm strip shows pulseless electrical activity

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next action?

options.text: Continue CPR for another 10 minutes before considering caesarean section
Perform bedside ultrasound to confirm fetal viability before deciding on caesarean
Transfer urgently to theatre for caesarean section under general anaesthesia
Cease resuscitation given likely amniotic fluid embolism or massive pulmonary embolism
Perimortem caesarean in resus bay at 11:06 (within 4 minutes of arrest), continue CPR

subtopic_detail: Placental abruption with fetal compromise at 34 weeks
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 woman at 34+5 weeks gestation presents to the obstetric assessment unit with sudden onset severe constant abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding starting 60 minutes ago. Her two previous deliveries were emergency caesarean sections. She has chronic hypertension managed on labetalol 200 mg twice daily; antenatal care has otherwise been uncomplicated and the fetus has been growing on the 50th centile.

On examination the uterus is tense, painful, and woody-hard to palpation. The cardiotocograph shows a sustained fetal bradycardia at 90 bpm with reduced variability. Vaginal examination reveals approximately 300 mL of dark blood, cervix posterior, 1 cm dilated, no cord felt. The patient is alert and oriented but anxious.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 110/min, BP 145/95 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C; fetal HR 90/min sustained
data_table.Examination: Tense painful woody uterus; CTG sustained fetal bradycardia 90 bpm reduced variability; vaginal exam 300 mL dark blood, cervix 1 cm posterior, no cord palpable
data_table.Investigations: Group and save sent; FBC haemoglobin 105 g/L (115-165), platelets 195 x10⁹/L (150-400); coagulation studies pending; bedside ultrasound shows retroplacental clot

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Activate massive transfusion protocol, two large bore IV cannulae, IV crystalloid resuscitation, and category 1 caesarean section within 30 minutes by the on call obstetric team
Perform immediate amniotomy to expedite assisted vaginal delivery with low cavity forceps once cervix is fully dilated under regional anaesthesia, with continuous CTG monitoring during birth
Commence tocolysis with nifedipine 20 mg orally and antenatal betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular before delivery to optimise fetal lung maturity before scheduling caesarean within 24 hours
Conservative management with strict bedrest, continuous CTG monitoring on the antenatal ward, and reassessment for delivery decision after 24 hours of observation and serial bloods
Attempt external cephalic version to confirm cephalic presentation followed by induction of labour with oxytocin and amniotomy under continuous CTG monitoring during the next 6 hours

stem:
A 29-year-old woman is seen in the fertility clinic with 18 months of primary infertility. She has oligomenorrhoea since menarche (4-6 cycles per year), hirsutism (modified Ferriman-Gallwey 12), and acne. Polycystic ovarian syndrome was diagnosed 4 years ago by Rotterdam criteria. Her body mass index is 33 kg/m². Over the past 6 months she has lost 8% of her body weight with dietitian and exercise physiologist input and has had 2 spontaneous cycles in that time.

Her male partner has a normal semen analysis. Hysterosalpingogram demonstrates patent fallopian tubes bilaterally. Her AMH is 78 pmol/L (3-30) and antral follicle count is 35 (12-25). Day 21 progesterone in her last cycle was 5 nmol/L (>30 confirms ovulation). She has no diabetes; HbA1c 5.1%.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 128/82 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: BMI 33; modified Ferriman-Gallwey 12; mild facial acne; no acanthosis nigricans; pelvic examination unremarkable; transvaginal ultrasound bilateral polycystic ovary morphology
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); prolactin 280 mIU/L (<500 non-pregnant); HbA1c 5.1%; AMH 78 pmol/L (3-30); 21-day progesterone 5 nmol/L (>30 ovulation confirmation)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line ovulation induction agent?

options.text: Clomifene citrate 50 mg orally days 2-6 of cycle for up to six ovulatory cycles with cycle monitoring by transvaginal ultrasound and day 21 progesterone
Letrozole 2.5 mg orally on days 2-6 of cycle for up to six ovulatory cycles with cycle monitoring by transvaginal ultrasound and day 21 progesterone for ovulation confirmation
Recombinant follicle stimulating hormone injection from day 2 of the cycle with cycle monitoring by transvaginal ultrasound and hCG trigger when lead follicle reaches 18 mm in diameter
Combined oral contraceptive pill for three months to suppress and reset the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, then a fourth cycle with hCG trigger after spontaneous follicle development
Refer for in vitro fertilisation with gonadotrophin releasing hormone antagonist protocol and elective single embryo transfer before any first-line ovulation induction trial in this couple

subtopic_detail: Acute uterine inversion - immediate replacement with placenta in situ
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P1 has just had a normal vaginal birth of a 4.0 kg infant after a prolonged second stage. Active management of the third stage was performed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU. Controlled cord traction was applied while the registrar assessed uterine tone, which was felt to be soft. Within seconds of traction the patient develops sudden severe abdominopelvic pain and looks pale.

On rapid reassessment her pulse is 38 beats per minute and blood pressure 65/30 mmHg. She remains conscious but distressed. Inspection of the perineum reveals an inverted boggy mass protruding through the introitus with the placenta still attached and approximately 600 mL of blood loss already documented. The anaesthetist is in the room.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38/min, BP 65/30 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale and distressed but conscious; abdominal palpation: uterine fundus not palpable; inverted boggy mass at introitus with attached placenta; estimated blood loss 600 mL ongoing
data_table.Investigations: FBC pre-delivery haemoglobin 122 g/L (115-165); group and save active; coagulation studies sent; no other investigations completed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Administer ergometrine 250 mcg intravenously immediately to contract the uterus before attempting replacement of the inverted fundus through the cervical ring during continuing resuscitation
Remove the placenta first by manual separation before attempting to replace the inverted uterus through the cervical ring as ongoing resuscitation continues with IV access and fluids
Immediate manual replacement of the uterine fundus via the Johnson manoeuvre with the placenta still attached, while resuscitating with IV fluids and giving atropine 600 mcg IV for vagal bradycardia
Urgent transfer to operating theatre for surgical replacement under general anaesthesia using the Huntington or Haultain procedure with no immediate attempt at manual replacement now
Bimanual uterine compression with intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes and packing of the inverted segment without any attempt at replacement during ongoing fluid resuscitation today

stem:
A 38-year-old G4P3 at 40+2 weeks gestation had labour induced for postdates pregnancy. She has just had a normal vaginal birth of a 3.6 kg infant. Within 90 seconds of placental delivery she becomes acutely dyspnoeic, agitated and complains of an impending sense of doom, then rapidly loses consciousness. The midwife notes ongoing brisk vaginal bleeding that does not clot when applied to gauze.

The anaesthetist intubates the patient. Brief cardiac compressions are commenced before pulses return with low-dose adrenaline. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a right heart strain pattern (S1Q3T3). Bedside echocardiogram performed by the intensivist shows a dilated right ventricle with septal flattening. There is no rash, no recent antibiotic exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min after adrenaline, BP 70/40 mmHg, RR ventilated, SpO2 88% on FiO2 1.0, temperature 36.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Intubated and ventilated; right heart strain on ECG and bedside echo with RV dilation and septal flattening; profuse non-clotting vaginal blood; estimated blood loss 1500 mL and rising
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (115-165), platelets 70 x10⁹/L (150-400), INR 2.4 (0.9-1.2), fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.5); group O Rh positive; cross-match in progress; troponin pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate blood-product strategy now?

options.text: Crystalloid resuscitation only with permissive hypotension targeting MAP 50 mmHg until cross matched packed red cells become available within the next 45 minutes from blood bank
Packed red blood cells alone targeting haemoglobin above 70 g/L without immediate fresh frozen plasma or cryoprecipitate until further coagulation studies are available for review by haematology
Packed red cells with one early unit of cryoprecipitate but defer fresh frozen plasma transfusion until repeat fibrinogen returns from the laboratory in approximately 30 minutes
Activate massive transfusion protocol with empirical 1:1:1 packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma and platelets, cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L, plus tranexamic acid 1 g IV
Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 25 units per kilogram intravenously as the sole haemostatic resuscitation strategy without balanced blood products until further investigations available

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman has just delivered a 4.1 kg baby vaginally at term in a tertiary obstetric unit after spontaneous labour. The third stage was actively managed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 units at delivery of the anterior shoulder. Twenty minutes after delivery she has lost an estimated 900 mL of blood and continues to bleed.

The uterus feels soft on bimanual examination and rises above the umbilicus despite massage. The placenta delivered complete and the perineum has been inspected with no significant tear. An intravenous oxytocin infusion has just been started at 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's at 250 mL/hour. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV has been administered. The maternal team is preparing the next uterotonic at the bedside. Her booking blood pressure was 118/74 and her booking medical history is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, BP 124/82 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus above umbilicus, perineum intact, no retained products on examination; cannulae 2 x 16G antecubital fossa, blood group and antibody screen sent
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin (pre-delivery) 120 g/L, platelets 220 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, fibrinogen 3.8 g/L (2.5-5.0); urine output measured by indwelling catheter; cross-match 4 units

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological uterotonic to give now?

options.text: Intravenous oxytocin 5 unit slow bolus repeated up to a total of 20 units in addition to the running oxytocin infusion already in progress at the bedside
Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms repeated every 15 minutes up to a maximum total dose of 2 mg before any other uterotonic is given to this patient
Intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms repeated at 15 minute intervals up to a maximum of 1 mg in 24 hours alongside the oxytocin infusion
Rectal misoprostol 800 micrograms by single dose and reassess uterine tone and ongoing blood loss again within the next 15 minutes after administration
Intramyometrial carbetocin 100 micrograms single dose injected directly through the abdominal wall under ultrasound guidance by the obstetric registrar urgently

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 27 weeks gestation attends a midwife-led shared-care clinic for a routine antenatal review. She has no significant past medical history and a BMI of 27 kg/m2. There is no family history of diabetes. The pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated and the dating ultrasound at 12 weeks was concordant with menstrual dates.

A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test was performed two days ago in the morning after an overnight fast. Fetal growth on most recent ultrasound is on the 50th centile, liquor volume normal, dopplers normal. Maternal blood pressure has been stable at booking values throughout. Symphysio-fundal height tracks with gestation. There is no proteinuria or glycosuria on dipstick today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, gravid uterus consistent with dates, fetal heart rate 142/min by Doppler, no oedema, no proteinuria on dipstick
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT (ADIPS): fasting 5.2 mmol/L (less than 5.1), 1 hour 9.8 mmol/L (less than 10.0), 2 hour 7.2 mmol/L (less than 8.5); HbA1c not performed; FBC and serum ferritin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test in 4 weeks' time to confirm a true diagnosis before any management changes are made to the pregnancy plan
Send a confirmatory HbA1c level to differentiate undiagnosed pre-existing type 2 diabetes from new-onset gestational diabetes mellitus before any further intervention
Reassure the patient that the OGTT is normal because the 1 hour and 2 hour values are well below the upper limit of the gestational diabetes diagnostic ranges
Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily empirically as first-line pharmacotherapy without trial of diet and exercise modification first and arrange MDT follow up
Diagnose gestational diabetes and arrange referral to the multidisciplinary diabetes-in-pregnancy team for dietary education and blood glucose self-monitoring

stem:
A 27-year-old G2P0 woman with blood group O Rhesus D negative presents to a metropolitan early pregnancy assessment clinic at 11 weeks gestation. She reports a single small painless bright red vaginal bleed yesterday with no associated pain. She had no previous antenatal anti-D administration in this pregnancy. Her first pregnancy ended in a 6 week miscarriage.

The abdomen is soft and non-tender on examination. A transvaginal ultrasound performed today shows a single live intrauterine pregnancy with a crown rump length consistent with 11 weeks and a 1 cm subchorionic haematoma. Fetal heart rate is 162 per minute. There is no cervical bleeding or open os on speculum examination. She has not started any anti-D yet in this pregnancy. Her antibody screen done at booking was negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no cervical motion tenderness, closed os on speculum; small subchorionic haematoma seen on TVUS
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O Rhesus D negative, antibody screen negative; haemoglobin 122 g/L; transvaginal ultrasound 11 week live intrauterine pregnancy with 1 cm subchorionic haematoma; quantitative bhCG not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding Rhesus D immunoprophylaxis?

options.text: Send fetal cell-free DNA Rhesus genotyping on a maternal sample and only administer anti-D once a Rhesus D positive fetus has been definitively confirmed
Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours of the bleed and document the dose on her antenatal record now
Hold anti-D immunoglobulin and reassess only at the next routine 28 week antenatal anti-D prophylaxis appointment if no further bleeding has occurred since today
Send a maternal Kleihauer-Betke test to determine the size of any feto-maternal haemorrhage and dose the anti-D based on the calculated feto-maternal bleed
