Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours of the bleed and document the dose on her antenatal record now

stem:
A 33-year-old G3P1 woman at 33+2 weeks gestation is brought to a tertiary maternity unit by her partner with severe occipital headache and visual scotomas that started 2 hours ago. She has been managed in pregnancy on oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily for chronic hypertension. The booking BP was 138/88 mmHg. Her renal function and liver enzymes were normal at last review one week ago.

On arrival her BP is markedly elevated on two readings five minutes apart on the same arm. She has 3+ proteinuria. The fetus is in cephalic presentation with reassuring CTG. Magnesium sulfate loading has just been started for seizure prophylaxis. Her last labetalol dose was 6 hours ago. She has no known asthma but does have an autoimmune Raynaud phenomenon documented in her past medical history. The obstetric team has called for urgent intravenous antihypertensive therapy to be drawn up.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 172/118 mmHg (repeated 168/116), RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C; fetal HR 140/min reassuring CTG
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes with 2 beats of clonus, no facial oedema, no right upper quadrant tenderness; visual fields intact to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 3+ protein, urine protein:creatinine ratio 320 mg/mmol (less than 30); platelets 142 x10^9/L, ALT 28 U/L (<35), creatinine 72 micromol/L; uric acid 0.42 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single best intravenous antihypertensive choice now?

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion at 5 micrograms per minute titrated to a target maternal mean arterial pressure of 100 mmHg in the resuscitation bay
Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus repeated and doubled every 10 minutes up to a maximum of 220 mg titrated against the maternal blood pressure response
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg immediate-release capsule and reassess the maternal blood pressure response after 30 minutes from administration in the resuscitation bay
Intravenous hydralazine 5 mg slow injection repeated every 20 minutes up to a maximum of 20 mg titrated against the maternal blood pressure response
Intravenous magnesium sulfate further 2 g bolus on top of the seizure prophylaxis loading dose targeted at lowering the maternal blood pressure to safe values

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P2 woman has been pushing for 50 minutes at full dilation in a tertiary delivery suite. Her two previous deliveries were uncomplicated vaginal births of 3.6 kg and 3.8 kg infants. Antenatal estimated fetal weight by growth scan one week ago was 4.4 kg; her booking BMI was 32 kg/m2. She has a diet-controlled gestational diabetes diagnosis from this pregnancy.

The fetal head delivers with classical turtling against the perineum. With gentle downward axial traction by the registrar the anterior shoulder will not deliver. The emergency buzzer has been pressed and the obstetric consultant, anaesthetist, neonatal team, and senior midwife are arriving. The clock has just started. The mother is positioned semi-recumbent at the edge of the bed. She is haemodynamically stable. The midwife is asking what the first manoeuvre should be.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102/min, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.2 °C; fetal HR 138/min by Doppler immediately after head delivery
data_table.Examination: Fetal head delivered with turtling against perineum, no spontaneous restitution; anterior shoulder impacted behind maternal pubic symphysis on gentle axial traction
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph was reassuring in second stage; no other investigations pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single best initial manoeuvre to attempt?

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal hips against the abdomen by two assistants standing on either side of the delivery bed
Apply suprapubic pressure aimed in the downward and lateral direction to dislodge the impacted anterior shoulder from behind the maternal pubic symphysis
Generous mediolateral episiotomy under local anaesthetic infiltration to enlarge the soft tissue space and allow direct access for the planned manoeuvres
Direct manual removal of the posterior arm of the fetus by sweeping it across the chest before any external manoeuvres have been attempted at this delivery
Apply firm downward fundal pressure by an assistant standing behind the maternal head to push the impacted anterior fetal shoulder downwards and forwards

subtopic_detail: Ovarian torsion diagnosis in normal Doppler
stem:
A 19-year-old nulliparous woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 8 hours of sudden onset severe right iliac fossa pain that began while she was at the gym doing burpees. She has vomited 4 times. The pain is constant with intermittent spikes. She is normally cycling, with her last menstrual period 12 days ago, and is sexually active using condoms.

On examination she is in significant pain at rest, lying still. The right iliac fossa is tender with voluntary guarding but no rebound. Her right adnexa is exquisitely tender on bimanual examination. Urine bhCG is negative. A transvaginal ultrasound reports a right ovary of 6.2 cm volume with a 3 cm haemorrhagic-appearing cyst, no free fluid in the pelvis, and preserved arterial and venous Doppler flow signals from the right ovarian vessels. The left ovary is normal at 4.1 cm volume. Pain control with oral oxycodone has not relieved her significantly.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding, exquisite right adnexal tenderness on bimanual; no peritonism, no cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine bhCG negative; haemoglobin 130 g/L, WCC 12.4 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L (<5); transvaginal ultrasound right ovary 6.2 cm volume with 3 cm haemorrhagic cyst, preserved arterial and venous Doppler signals; urine microscopy bland

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home with oral analgesia and arrange outpatient gynaecology review in 1 week given that ultrasound Doppler signals from the right ovary are preserved
Trial of intravenous opiate analgesia and antispasmodic medication and reassessment of clinical signs and pain scores after 2 hours of adequate analgesia first
Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound with Doppler in 4 to 6 hours to look for any interval change in arterial or venous flow signals or any size increase
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with contrast to clarify the ovarian appearances and viability before a final surgical decision is made by gynaecology
Urgent diagnostic laparoscopy by the gynaecology team aiming for ovarian detorsion and conservation regardless of macroscopic appearance at first inspection

stem:
A 36-year-old G4P3 woman is reviewed in a tertiary maternal-fetal medicine clinic at 30 weeks gestation. She has had three previous caesarean sections without complication and is now booked for a fourth planned caesarean. The current pregnancy is uncomplicated. Fetal growth is on the 50th centile. Her booking BMI is 28 kg/m2 and she is otherwise well.

A detailed ultrasound at 28 weeks describes an anterior placenta covering the internal cervical os. The report flags loss of the retroplacental clear zone, two large placental lacunae with turbulent flow, and bridging vessels between the placenta and the bladder. A confirmatory MRI shows myometrial thinning to 1 mm between the placenta and the bladder, focal bulging of the placenta into the bladder serosa, but no clear breach of the bladder wall itself. She has been counselled that planned delivery will be early.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6 °C; fetal HR 142/min reassuring
data_table.Examination: Gravid uterus consistent with 30 weeks; no abdominal tenderness; symphysio-fundal height 30 cm; no vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound and MRI consistent with placenta percreta involving bladder serosa; haemoglobin 118 g/L, ferritin 24 mcg/L (15-200), platelets 232 x10^9/L, group and antibody screen negative; cell saver and urology available at the tertiary unit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate planned mode and timing of delivery to recommend at the multidisciplinary planning meeting?

options.text: Spontaneous vaginal delivery at term with continuous CTG monitoring and active management of the third stage including immediate manual removal of placenta
Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 weeks gestation at a tertiary centre with multidisciplinary team, cell saver, urology back-up, and antenatal corticosteroids
Planned caesarean section at 39 weeks gestation with attempted manual placental removal followed by uterotonics and balloon tamponade if heavy bleeding ensues
Planned caesarean section at 37 weeks gestation with placenta left in situ and outpatient methotrexate therapy aiming for delayed resorption over 6 months postpartum
Planned classical caesarean section at 32 weeks gestation followed by uterine artery embolisation in the angiography suite as planned definitive haemorrhage control

subtopic_detail: VBAC counselling after one prior LSCS
stem:
A 32-year-old woman in her second pregnancy attends a 36-week midwife-led antenatal review. Her first child was delivered by emergency caesarean three years ago at 39 weeks gestation for a non-reassuring CTG in early labour. There were no complications during recovery, and she has had no other surgical procedures. This pregnancy has been uncomplicated.

She weighs 76 kg with a booking BMI of 26. The current pregnancy is singleton, cephalic, with an estimated fetal weight at the 50th centile. Placental position is fundal-posterior on the 32-week scan. Her midwife refers her to the obstetric clinic to discuss mode of birth. She tells you she is keen to attempt a vaginal birth this time but is worried about uterine rupture.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: fundal height 36 cm, cephalic, longitudinal lie, fetal heart 140 bpm
data_table.Investigations: 32-week ultrasound: singleton cephalic, EFW at 50th centile, fundal-posterior placenta

lead_in: What is the most accurate counselling regarding planned vaginal birth after caesarean?

options.text: Vaginal birth success approximately 30 percent; uterine rupture risk approximately 5 percent
Vaginal birth success approximately 60 percent; uterine rupture risk approximately 2 percent
Vaginal birth success approximately 70 percent; uterine rupture risk approximately 0.5 percent
Vaginal birth success approximately 90 percent; uterine rupture risk approximately 0.1 percent
Vaginal birth contraindicated; recommend elective repeat caesarean at 39 weeks gestation

stem:
A 29-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends for routine antenatal screening at 27 weeks gestation. She has no personal or family history of diabetes. Booking BMI was 24 and she has gained 9 kg in pregnancy so far. The pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated, with normal morphology scan and a singleton cephalic fetus tracking the 55th centile for estimated weight.

She completes a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test as outpatient. Results: fasting venous plasma glucose 5.3 mmol/L, 1-hour 9.4 mmol/L, 2-hour 7.6 mmol/L. She is asymptomatic. Vital signs are within normal limits. Urine dipstick is negative for protein, glucose, and ketones.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: uterus appropriate for dates, fetal heart 145 bpm, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: 75g OGTT: fasting 5.3 mmol/L, 1-h 9.4 mmol/L, 2-h 7.6 mmol/L; urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?

options.text: Normal pregnancy; repeat OGTT at 32 weeks if clinical concerns arise
Impaired glucose tolerance; arrange repeat 75 g OGTT in 6 weeks for confirmation
Pre-existing type 2 diabetes; commence insulin and refer to endocrinology
Gestational diabetes; commence dietary advice, monitoring, and diabetes referral
Borderline result; lifestyle advice only with no formal diabetes referral

stem:
A 28-year-old woman, blood group O Rhesus-negative, presents to the early pregnancy assessment unit at 11+3 weeks gestation with one day of light per-vaginal bleeding and mild lower abdominal cramping. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated and resulted in a vaginal birth two years ago, after which she received post-natal anti-D 625 IU.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable. Speculum reveals a closed cervical os with a small amount of dark blood in the vault. Bimanual examination is unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates a singleton intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal pole and cardiac activity at a gestational age of 11+4 weeks. Her partner is known to be Rhesus-positive. Indirect Coombs test confirms she has no detectable anti-D antibodies.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: speculum closed os with small dark blood; bimanual unremarkable; abdomen non-tender
data_table.Investigations: TVS singleton IUP with cardiac activity at 11+4 wk; indirect Coombs negative; blood group O Rh-negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immunoglobulin management?

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours of bleeding
Anti-D immunoglobulin 1500 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours of bleeding
No anti-D required for threatened miscarriage with closed os under 12 weeks
Defer anti-D and arrange Kleihauer-Betke test to quantify feto-maternal haemorrhage
Anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours of bleeding

subtopic_detail: Mode of delivery for DCDA twins at 37 weeks
stem:
A 31-year-old primigravida with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy attends a 36-week obstetric review. Both fetuses are alive and growing concordantly, with estimated fetal weights at the 50th and 55th centiles and an inter-twin discordance of 6 percent. She has no medical co-morbidities and the pregnancy has been uncomplicated.

On examination her symphysis-fundal height is 42 cm. Twin 1 is cephalic with engaged presenting part; twin 2 is transverse with the fetal back inferior. Cervical examination reveals a closed, posterior cervix. Both placentas are fundal-anterior on the most recent ultrasound, with normal umbilical artery Doppler. She is keen to plan a vaginal birth at 37+5 weeks gestation, the unit's standard timing for DCDA twins.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: SFH 42 cm; twin 1 cephalic engaged; twin 2 transverse; cervix closed posterior
data_table.Investigations: 36-wk ultrasound: DCDA twins, EFW 50th and 55th centile (6% discordance), fundal-anterior placentas, normal umbilical Doppler

lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling regarding mode of birth?

options.text: Recommend elective caesarean at 37+5 weeks because twin 2 is non-cephalic
Plan vaginal birth at 37+5 weeks with internal podalic version of twin 2 in labour
Plan vaginal birth at 38+5 weeks regardless of twin 2 presentation in labour
Defer delivery decision until spontaneous labour and manage twin 2 in labour
Recommend elective caesarean at 36+0 weeks due to twin pregnancy risk profile

subtopic_detail: Timing of caesarean for asymptomatic placenta praevia
stem:
A 35-year-old multigravida (G3 P2) attends antenatal clinic at 34+5 weeks gestation. A transabdominal scan at 32 weeks identified placenta praevia with the placental edge covering the internal cervical os by 18 mm. A repeat transvaginal scan at 34 weeks confirmed a major praevia with the lower edge 12 mm across the os. She has had no per-vaginal bleeding throughout the pregnancy.

On examination she is well, vital signs within normal limits, with a soft non-tender abdomen. The fetus is in transverse lie with an estimated fetal weight at the 50th centile. Her previous two deliveries were uncomplicated vaginal births. The pregnancy is otherwise low-risk and she has had antenatal corticosteroids in a prior preterm threatened labour at 31 weeks (fetus born at term).

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: soft non-tender abdomen, fetus transverse, no per-vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: TVS at 34 weeks: placenta covering internal os by 12 mm (major praevia), EFW 50th centile, normal umbilical Doppler

lead_in: What is the most appropriate elective delivery plan?

options.text: Schedule elective lower-segment caesarean at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks gestation
Schedule elective lower-segment caesarean at 39+0 weeks gestation
Schedule elective lower-segment caesarean at 34+0 weeks gestation
Plan trial of labour with continuous CTG and an experienced obstetrician on standby
Repeat ultrasound at 37 weeks before deciding on delivery timing

subtopic_detail: Management of PPROM at 34 to 36 weeks (RANZCOG)
stem:
A 27-year-old primigravida at 34+5 weeks gestation presents with a 4-hour history of clear fluid loss per vaginam. She felt a small gush followed by ongoing dampness. There is no abdominal pain, no per-vaginal bleeding, and the fetus is moving normally.

On examination she is afebrile with pulse 78, blood pressure 118 by 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Speculum reveals a pool of clear fluid in the posterior fornix that ferns on slide testing. The cervix is closed. CTG shows a baseline of 140 with normal variability and accelerations. White cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4-11) and CRP 4 mg/L (<5). Group B streptococcus screen at 28 weeks was negative.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: speculum: clear fluid pool, ferning positive, cervix closed; abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: WCC 9.2 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 4 mg/L (<5), GBS negative at 28 wk, CTG baseline 140 normal variability with accelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Admit, commence IV benzylpenicillin and erythromycin and induce labour with oxytocin now
Admit, latency erythromycin and expectant management with daily CTG and inflammatory markers
Discharge home on oral amoxicillin with daily clinic review and self-temperature monitoring
Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM and proceed to elective caesarean at 35+0 weeks
Administer tocolysis with nifedipine and continue surveillance until 37 weeks gestation

subtopic_detail: Ectopic in only remaining tube after prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
A 33-year-old woman G2 P0 presents to the early pregnancy assessment service with three days of right iliac fossa pain and a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. Three years ago she had an emergency laparoscopic left salpingectomy for a ruptured ectopic pregnancy; she has no other gynaecological surgery and no children. She would like to preserve every reasonable chance of future spontaneous conception.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable. Abdomen is soft with mild right iliac fossa tenderness without peritonism. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a 3 cm right adnexal mass containing a yolk sac but no fetal cardiac activity, with a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum bhCG is 2400 IU/L. FBC, group and hold, and electrolytes are within normal limits. The left ovary is structurally normal and the left tube is absent on imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: abdomen soft with mild RIF tenderness, no peritonism, no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: TVS: empty uterus, 3 cm right adnexal mass with yolk sac, no cardiac activity, small free fluid in pouch of Douglas; bhCG 2400 IU/L; left tube absent (prior salpingectomy)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical procedure if she opts for operative management?

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingostomy with conservative tube preservation
Methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM single-dose protocol with weekly bhCG follow-up
Laparoscopic ipsilateral oophorectomy with tubal preservation
Laparoscopic right salpingectomy with histopathology of the resected tube
Laparotomy with right salpingectomy and contralateral tube preservation review

stem:
A 36-year-old woman attends your general practice for a routine cervical screening test. She has had previous normal screening tests at age 30 and 25; she has no symptoms of abnormal bleeding and is not pregnant. She is up to date with HPV vaccination from school years. She has been with the same partner for 8 years.

The self-collected vaginal swab returns oncogenic HPV (non 16, non 18) positive. A reflex liquid-based cytology from the same sample reports low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL).

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: asymptomatic; speculum examination not performed for self-collected screen
data_table.Investigations: HPV PCR: oncogenic non 16/18 detected; reflex LBC: LSIL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in screening management?

options.text: Refer urgently for colposcopy and directed biopsy within 8 weeks
Repeat the cervical screening test in 12 months as intermediate risk
Repeat cervical screening test in 5 years as standard low-risk recall
Refer for endometrial sampling and a pelvic ultrasound at this visit
Prescribe topical imiquimod and recheck cytology in 6 months from now

stem:
A 24-year-old woman attends your general practice for advice about irregular periods and growing dark hair on her chin and lower abdomen over the past two years. Her periods come every 50 to 70 days. Her BMI is 28. She is not on contraception and is currently sexually active with a male partner.

Clinical examination confirms terminal hair on the chin, around the umbilicus, and on the lower back. There is no acanthosis nigricans. Pelvic ultrasound was performed last week; the report describes both ovaries containing more than 20 antral follicles 2 to 9 mm in diameter, with normal stromal volume.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: modified Ferriman-Gallwey score 10, BMI 28 kg/m^2, no virilising features such as clitoromegaly or deepened voice
data_table.Investigations: fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4); total testosterone 2.6 nmol/L (less than 2.0); SHBG 28 nmol/L; prolactin 280 mIU/L (less than 500); TSH 1.8 mIU/L; 17-hydroxyprogesterone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in confirming the diagnosis?

options.text: Order serum DHEAS, androstenedione, and a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test
Repeat pelvic ultrasound in 3 months to confirm ovarian morphology
Diagnose PCOS and counsel on lifestyle plus long-term metabolic risk
Request an MRI of the adrenals and ovaries to exclude an androgen-secreting tumour
Defer the diagnosis pending a 2-hour 75 g oral glucose tolerance test

stem:
A 23-year-old woman attends with painful periods that have worsened over the past two years. The pain starts the day before her period, peaks on day 2, and stops her attending university for 1 to 2 days each cycle. She also has deep pain during intercourse. She has never been pregnant and is not currently planning pregnancy; she uses condoms for contraception.

General and pelvic examination are unremarkable. There is no adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination and no nodularity is felt on rectovaginal palpation. She has tried ibuprofen with limited effect. She has no contraindications to combined hormonal contraception (no smoking history, no migraine with aura, no thrombotic risk factors, normal blood pressure).

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: normal vulva and vagina, soft non-tender cervix, no adnexal mass, no rectovaginal nodularity
data_table.Investigations: transvaginal ultrasound: normal-sized anteverted uterus, no endometrioma, ovaries normal volume, no deep infiltrating lesions identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for diagnostic laparoscopy as the first management step
Trial a continuous combined oral contraceptive pill plus regular ibuprofen
Commence a 3-month course of GnRH agonist with hormonal add-back therapy
Reassure her that primary dysmenorrhoea is benign and review in 12 months
Order serum CA-125 to confirm or exclude an endometriosis diagnosis

stem:
A 62-year-old woman attends your practice with a single episode of light vaginal bleeding three days ago, the first since her menopause at age 53. She is otherwise well, takes no medication, has never used hormone replacement therapy, and is not on tamoxifen. Her BMI is 34 and she has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin.

On examination there is no obvious vulval or vaginal lesion, the cervix appears healthy, and bimanual examination is unremarkable. There is no active bleeding at the time of review. Cervical screening is up to date and negative.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: atrophic vulva and vagina, healthy cervix, no adnexal mass, no rectovaginal nodularity
data_table.Investigations: transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 7 mm with irregular endomyometrial junction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months for surveillance
Reassure that one episode of bleeding does not require investigation
Commence vaginal oestrogen for atrophy and review in 6 months
Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy with directed endometrial biopsy
Order an MRI pelvis to characterise the endometrium before any sampling

subtopic_detail: Pulmonary oedema after fluid administration in severe pre-eclampsia
stem: A 31-year-old woman with severe pre-eclampsia gave birth six hours ago. She has received three litres of crystalloid since admission and remains on a magnesium sulfate infusion. She is now breathless sitting upright.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 148/92, pulse 112, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 89% room air
data_table.Examination: Fine inspiratory crackles to the mid-zones; patellar reflexes present and brisk
data_table.Investigations: Urine output 20 mL per hour; creatinine 88 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oxygen, stop intravenous fluids and give furosemide 40 mg intravenously
Oxygen, give a 250 mL crystalloid fluid challenge and reassess her output
Oxygen, stop the magnesium and give calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL
Oxygen, give intravenous hydralazine 5 mg and repeat after 20 minutes
Oxygen, start therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg and arrange a CT scan

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 36+5 weeks attends antenatal clinic having been told at her routine appointment last week that the baby was breech. The previous delivery was an uncomplicated vaginal birth of a cephalic baby at 39 weeks. She has no significant past medical history and the current pregnancy has been uncomplicated.

Today's ultrasound confirms frank breech presentation with an estimated fetal weight on the 60th centile, normal liquor volume (deepest vertical pocket 5 cm), anterior placenta not low lying, and reassuring umbilical artery Doppler. The CTG performed on arrival is reassuring. There is no history of antepartum haemorrhage, no uterine scar, and she has not yet decided on her birth plan.

data_table.Vital signs: maternal vital signs within normal limits; fetal heart rate baseline 138 /min, reactive CTG
data_table.Examination: soft non-tender abdomen, fundal height 36 cm, breech palpable in the pelvis, fetal heart auscultated in upper quadrant
data_table.Investigations: ultrasound: frank breech, EFW 60th centile, DVP 5 cm, anterior placenta not low lying, UA Doppler normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for moxibustion at acupuncture points BL67 as the first intervention
Book elective caesarean section at 39 weeks without offering ECV
Recommend immediate vaginal breech delivery planning given multiparity
Trial a knee-to-chest position three times daily and review in 2 weeks
Offer external cephalic version at 37 weeks with tocolysis after counselling

stem:
A 27-year-old G2P1 woman at 28+4 weeks presents to the birthing unit with a sudden gush of clear fluid one hour ago, followed by ongoing leaking. There are no contractions, no per vaginal bleeding, and fetal movements are normal. Her previous pregnancy ended in spontaneous vaginal delivery at term.

Sterile speculum confirms pooling of clear fluid in the posterior fornix. Cervix appears closed; no digital examination is performed. Maternal observations and CTG are reassuring. Ultrasound shows oligohydramnios with a deepest vertical pocket of 1.8 cm; estimated fetal weight is on the 45th centile; the fetus is cephalic. There are no clinical features of chorioamnionitis (no fever, uterine tenderness, or offensive discharge).

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: no contractions, soft non-tender uterus, sterile speculum shows pooling of clear amniotic fluid
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 9.8 x10^9/L (4 to 11); CRP 6 mg/L; high vaginal swab and urine culture sent; CTG reassuring; group B streptococcus status unknown

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management bundle?

options.text: Induce labour immediately with oxytocin to minimise infection risk
Admit for IM betamethasone, oral erythromycin, and IV magnesium for neuroprotection
Admit, give a single dose of dexamethasone, and start IV amoxicillin with clavulanic acid for 10 days
Discharge home on oral metronidazole with daily fetal movement counting
Perform a digital cervical examination to plan timing of induction

stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida is admitted to the birth suite at 34 plus 2 weeks gestation with a 24 hour history of a frontal headache and 'spots' in her vision. She has been monitored as an outpatient for proteinuria (1+) since 30 weeks. Her partner says she was confused for a few minutes at home but recovered before they arrived.

On examination she is alert and oriented now. Knee jerks are 3+ and symmetrical. The uterus is non-tender, the cervix is closed on speculum, and the cardiotocograph baseline is 140 with two accelerations and no decelerations over a 30 minute trace. Her partner reports she had a single self-limiting tonic-clonic seizure on the corridor as they walked into the assessment area, lasting 90 seconds. Maternal vital signs and bloods are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 102, blood pressure 172/112, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees, fetal heart rate 140
data_table.Investigations: platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 142 U/L (<40), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), urine protein:creatinine 320 mg/mmol (<30), lactate dehydrogenase 612 U/L, haptoglobin within normal limits, urate 0.42 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate caesarean section without antiseizure prophylaxis on the basis that delivery is the definitive cure for eclampsia
Intravenous diazepam 10 mg bolus and intravenous phenytoin loading at 18 mg/kg, with antihypertensive therapy afterward
Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour, with labetalol to target blood pressure under 160/110
Intravenous hydralazine 5 mg bolus every 20 minutes targeting blood pressure under 130/80 without antiseizure prophylaxis
Commence intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg and admit for outpatient blood pressure and proteinuria surveillance

stem:
A 33-year-old G3P2 woman has just delivered a 3.9 kg baby by spontaneous vaginal birth at 40 plus 3 weeks after a four hour active second stage. She received active third stage management with 10 units intramuscular oxytocin. The placenta delivered complete at 12 minutes. Twenty minutes after delivery she has soaked through two large pads with fresh red blood and a third is in progress. The midwife has called for help and started bimanual uterine massage.

On examination the uterus is large and soft despite massage. There is no perineal or vaginal wall tear on inspection, the cervix appears intact, and the placenta is confirmed complete. Two 16 gauge cannulas are in. Her booking blood pressure was 132/86 and antenatal blood pressure has remained around 135/85 throughout pregnancy. She has no asthma. Vital signs are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 116, blood pressure 102/64, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees
data_table.Investigations: estimated blood loss 1100 mL and ongoing, haemoglobin pre-delivery 124 g/L, group and screen on file, fibrinogen pending

lead_in: After ongoing uterine massage and an infusion of oxytocin 40 units in 1 L normal saline, which is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost (15-methyl PGF2 alpha) 250 micrograms with intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes
Intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms with concurrent intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes
Sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms with intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes for tone augmentation
Intravenous oxytocin further bolus of 10 units repeated every five minutes until uterine tone is restored
Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms with concurrent insertion of an intrauterine Bakri balloon for tamponade

stem:
A 36-year-old G2P1 woman of South Asian background is reviewed at the joint obstetric-endocrine clinic at 30 weeks gestation. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks on a positive 75 g OGTT. She has completed two weeks of structured dietitian-led carbohydrate counselling and 30 minutes of post-meal walking. She is monitoring fasting and one hour post-meal capillary blood glucose four times per day.

Her body mass index pre-pregnancy was 27.6 kg/m^2. Fetal growth ultrasound at 28 weeks showed abdominal circumference on the 78th centile and estimated fetal weight on the 72nd centile. There has been no maternal hypoglycaemia. She has no proteinuria, normal blood pressure, and no obstetric or medical contraindications to oral therapy or insulin. The seven-day capillary record is summarised below.

data_table.Investigations: fasting glucose 24 of 28 readings above 5.0 mmol/L (range 4.9 to 6.4), one hour post-meal glucose 18 of 63 readings above 7.4 mmol/L (range 5.6 to 8.8), HbA1c at diagnosis 5.4 percent, no ketonuria, urine albumin:creatinine ratio normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lifestyle and dietary measures alone with reassessment of capillary blood glucose readings in two weeks
Commence rapid acting insulin aspart 4 units subcutaneously before each main meal only without basal coverage
Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily with a stop date if fetal growth accelerates beyond the 95th centile on scan
Commence basal insulin (isophane or detemir) 0.1 to 0.2 units/kg subcutaneously at bedtime and titrate to fasting target
Commence glibenclamide 2.5 mg orally daily and continue dietetic review monthly for the remainder of pregnancy

stem:
A 34-year-old woman attends general practice asking to restart the combined oral contraceptive pill after a four year gap. She is otherwise well, a non-smoker, with a body mass index of 24.6 kg/m^2 and no personal history of venous thromboembolism. Her mother had a deep vein thrombosis at age 58 following an orthopaedic operation but no younger relatives are affected.

She has migraine with aura twice a year (visual scintillations followed by unilateral throbbing headache) which respond to oral sumatriptan. Her last episode was six weeks ago. Blood pressure is 122/78. She has had three normal cervical screening test results and no abnormal bleeding. She does not want a long-acting reversible contraceptive method and has not had children.

data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 134 g/L, thyroid function within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative, blood pressure repeated 122/78

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a 30 microgram levonorgestrel combined oral contraceptive pill from day one of her next menstrual period
Refer for full thrombophilia screening before deciding on a combined hormonal method or a progestogen-only method
Commence the combined vaginal ring on the basis that lower systemic oestrogen exposure is safe in migraine with aura
Continue with a combined oral contraceptive but advise her to stop immediately if she has another migraine with aura
Commence the progestogen-only desogestrel pill 75 micrograms daily or recommend depot medroxyprogesterone instead

stem:
A 28-year-old G3P2 woman presents to the maternity assessment unit at 32 weeks gestation with a sudden 200 mL fresh bright red vaginal bleed at home that has now slowed. She is not in pain. Her two previous births were both caesareans for breech and arrest. She has had no abdominal trauma. Her partner reports that she was hanging washing when the bleed started.

On examination she is alert and pink. The uterus is soft and non-tender to palpation. She has not had a speculum examination in this unit yet. The mid-trimester morphology scan (booking the dates the booking ultrasound recorded at 20 weeks) reported a low-lying anterior placenta with a placental edge covering the internal os; a follow-up scan has not yet been performed. Vital signs are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 96, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees, fetal heart rate 142 on intermittent Doppler
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 112 g/L, group and antibody screen on file (group O Rh negative, antibody negative), repeat group and screen and crossmatch 4 units sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent transvaginal ultrasound to localise the placenta, admit, give betamethasone 11.4 mg, and give anti-D 625 IU
Digital cervical examination in the assessment room to determine cervical dilatation and station before any imaging
Discharge home with weekly outpatient cardiotocography after the bleeding settles and plan vaginal birth at full term
Proceed directly to category 1 caesarean section without imaging because of the painless fresh red vaginal bleeding
Insert a cervical tamponade balloon to reduce ongoing bleeding before further imaging or specialist obstetric review

stem:
A 30-year-old G3P0+2 woman attends a high risk antenatal clinic at 18 weeks gestation. Her two previous pregnancies ended at 21 and 23 weeks with painless cervical dilatation and bulging membranes followed by spontaneous preterm birth and neonatal death. There is no history of cervical surgery or LLETZ. The current dating ultrasound was concordant with menstrual dates.

On examination the abdomen is soft and there is no contraction. A transvaginal ultrasound today shows a singleton with normal anatomy and a cervical length of 18 mm with funnelling at the internal os. There are no signs of intra-amniotic infection: she is afebrile, the maternal CRP is 4 mg/L, white cells 9.2 x10^9/L, and there is no discharge. The vaginal swab and urine culture are negative.

data_table.Investigations: cervical length 18 mm, funnelling at internal os, fetus appropriate for dates with normal anatomy, no membrane prolapse, CRP 4 mg/L (<5), white cells 9.2 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an emergency rescue cervical cerclage today even though the membranes are not prolapsed and cervix is closed
Insert an Arabin cervical pessary and avoid surgical cerclage to minimise procedural and anaesthetic risk for her
Commence weekly intramuscular 17 hydroxyprogesterone caproate as monotherapy in the second and third trimester
Recommend strict bed rest in hospital until 34 weeks gestation without procedural intervention or progesterone
Schedule an ultrasound indicated transvaginal cervical cerclage and continue vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman with an in-vitro fertilisation singleton pregnancy reaches 35 plus 4 weeks gestation. Her morphology scan reported a velamentous cord insertion with a bilobed placenta, and a third trimester scan at 32 weeks confirmed a vessel running across the internal cervical os without supporting placental tissue. She has been admitted at 34 weeks for surveillance and completed a course of antenatal corticosteroids.

This afternoon she has a brisk fresh red vaginal bleed of about 100 mL after her membranes ruptured spontaneously. The midwife describes the liquor as port-wine coloured. She has no abdominal pain and the uterus is soft. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 110 falling to 90 with a sinusoidal pattern over the past four minutes. Her vital signs are stable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, fetal heart rate 110 with sinusoidal pattern
data_table.Investigations: maternal full blood count and coagulation within normal limits, group and screen on file, Apt test of vaginal blood positive for fetal haemoglobin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Augment labour with intravenous oxytocin aiming for vaginal birth given the gestation of 35 plus 4 weeks today
Immediate category 1 caesarean section with the neonatal resuscitation team and uncrossmatched O negative blood ready
Insert an intrauterine pressure catheter and observe with continuous cardiotocography over the next sixty minutes
Administer maternal intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g and reassess the fetal heart trace in fifteen minutes' time
Repeat the Apt test on vaginal blood in 15 minutes and proceed to caesarean only if it is positive a second time

subtopic_detail: Selective fetal growth restriction in MCDA twins
stem:
A 27-year-old G2P1 woman with a monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA) twin pregnancy is reviewed at the maternal fetal medicine clinic at 26 plus 5 weeks. Both twins were grown concordantly at the 18 week scan. The 24 week scan showed an estimated fetal weight discordance of 22 percent. Today's scan shows further discordance.

Twin A is appropriately grown on the 35th centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler. Twin B is on the 4th centile with an intermittent absent end-diastolic flow pattern in the umbilical artery that cycles between forward, absent, and reversed (positive then negative then positive) every several minutes when watched for 15 minutes. The middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is within normal limits in both twins. Amniotic fluid volumes are normal in both sacs. Maternal blood pressure is normal and there is no proteinuria.

data_table.Investigations: twin A estimated fetal weight 35th centile, umbilical artery PI within normal limits; twin B estimated fetal weight 4th centile, intermittent absent and reversed end-diastolic flow (Gratacos type III); middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocities within normal limits in both; amniotic fluid normal in both sacs; no anatomical anomalies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Plan elective caesarean section at 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids and weekly outpatient surveillance
Refer to a tertiary maternal fetal medicine unit for fetoscopic laser ablation or selective bipolar cord occlusion
Administer maternal oral sildenafil to augment placental perfusion in the growth restricted twin from this week
Commence weekly outpatient cardiotocography and repeat umbilical artery Doppler assessment again in two weeks
Deliver both twins by emergency caesarean section today at 26 plus 5 weeks regardless of viability considerations

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P3 has just had a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39+5 weeks of a 4.1 kg baby with rapid third stage. Her booking pregnancy was complicated by pregnancy-induced hypertension and she has been on oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily since 32 weeks with home blood pressures around 138/86. Her placenta delivered apparently intact ten minutes ago.

On assessment now her uterus is boggy at the umbilicus despite fundal massage and she has had 800 mL of fresh red blood loss into the drape in the last 15 minutes. The midwife has called for senior review and a second wide-bore intravenous line is being placed. She is alert but pale and clammy. The placenta has been re-examined and looks complete with intact cotyledons and membranes. There is no vaginal or perineal laceration on inspection.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 110, blood pressure 95/60, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees

lead_in: Which uterotonic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscular as first line and a 40 unit oxytocin infusion in 1000 mL Hartmann's over four hours
Sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms with intrauterine vaginal packing in the delivery room while awaiting senior review
Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscular every fifteen minutes for up to eight doses as primary uterotonic for atony
Oxytocin 10 units intramuscular plus a 40 unit oxytocin infusion in 1000 mL Hartmann's over four hours, and intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g
Bakri balloon insertion at the bedside and immediate transfer to the operating theatre for examination under anaesthesia

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis with penicillin allergy
stem:
A 28-year-old G2P1 at 38+0 weeks presents to delivery suite in early labour. Her vaginal-rectal screening swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus. She has a previous vaginal delivery at 39 weeks without complications. Her first child had no neonatal sepsis. She is otherwise well.

She tells you she developed a generalised pruritic rash and lip swelling when prescribed amoxicillin two years ago for tonsillitis and was told to avoid penicillins by the emergency department doctor at the time. She has not had any antibiotic since then. She is currently 4 cm dilated with regular contractions and ruptured membranes one hour ago at home. The midwife has commenced intravenous access and a syntocinon augmentation has not yet been started.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees, fetal heart rate 142 with normal variability

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous clindamycin 600 mg every eight hours from now until delivery, confirming GBS susceptibility on the laboratory antibiogram
Intravenous cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every eight hours until delivery, after a graded penicillin challenge in labour
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every four hours until delivery, with adrenaline drawn up at the bedside
Oral cefalexin 500 mg every six hours until delivery and a single intravenous dose at the time of delivery to cover the neonate
No antibiotics required because she had a previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery and the colony count is unknown

subtopic_detail: Pregnancy of uncertain viability and Anti-D
stem:
A 25-year-old G1P0 at 7+2 weeks by last menstrual period presents to early pregnancy unit with 24 hours of light vaginal bleeding and mild lower abdominal cramps. She has had no syncopal episodes and no shoulder tip pain. Her blood group on a booking blood test today is documented as RhD negative.

On examination her observations are normal. Speculum reveals a closed cervical os with a small amount of dark blood pooling in the posterior fornix. Bimanual examination shows a soft anteverted uterus, no cervical motion tenderness, and no adnexal mass or tenderness. There has been no previous miscarriage and she conceived spontaneously. There is no significant past gynaecological history and she takes no medications.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 84, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: serum beta-hCG 14000 IU/L, transvaginal ultrasound: single intrauterine gestational sac with yolk sac and embryo with crown-rump length 3.5 mm, no fetal cardiac activity demonstrated, no adnexal mass, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous antibiotics and uterine evacuation in theatre for a presumed septic incomplete miscarriage with retained products
Administer intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m squared and arrange serial beta-hCG measurements every 48 hours for one week
Discharge home with repeat transvaginal ultrasound and beta-hCG in 7 to 10 days, give Anti-D 250 IU intramuscular, and provide written safety netting advice
Commence vaginal misoprostol 800 micrograms now and a second dose at 24 hours for medical management of a missed miscarriage
Admit for 48 hour observation and offer dilatation and curettage if vaginal bleeding has not stopped by review the following morning

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 at 35+2 weeks self-presents to triage with two hours of frontal headache, blurry vision with scotomata, and epigastric pain. Her booking blood pressure was 118/74 and her antenatal record shows no prior hypertension. Fetal movements have been normal today.

On examination she is alert and orientated. There is mild hyperreflexia at the knees without clonus. There is no peripheral oedema and no rash. Urine dipstick is 3+ protein. Cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 140 with normal variability and no decelerations. Speculum is not yet performed. Her observation chart is shown below. There is no abdominal tenderness on uterine palpation between contractions and no PV bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 102, blood pressure 168/112, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-145), platelets 142 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 80 U/L (<35), urate 0.42 mmol/L (<0.36), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), urine protein:creatinine ratio 220 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral nifedipine 20 mg now, repeat in thirty minutes if blood pressure is not below 150/100, and arrange emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia
Intravenous labetalol infusion alone and tocolysis with nifedipine to prolong gestation by 48 hours for corticosteroid completion
Oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily and outpatient antenatal day-assessment unit review in twenty four hours for blood pressure trend
Intravenous diazepam 10 mg slow bolus for seizure prophylaxis and intravenous hydralazine 5 mg boluses every twenty minutes
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion plus intravenous labetalol for blood pressure control, and admit

subtopic_detail: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 32 weeks
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 at 32+1 weeks presents to delivery suite four hours after a sudden gush of clear fluid at home. She has no contractions. Her pregnancy has been low risk and she is fully vaccinated including booster pertussis. Her 35-week vaginal-rectal swab is not yet due. Booking blood group is A positive.

On examination she is well and afebrile. Speculum demonstrates clear amniotic pooling in the posterior fornix with a closed cervix. There is no offensive odour and the umbilical cord is not visible. Fetal cardiotocograph shows baseline 138 with normal variability, no contractions, and no decelerations. Ultrasound estimates the fetus is in a cephalic presentation with normal liquor outside the membrane defect, and weight on the 60th centile. She has no allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 86, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: white cells 11.0 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 8 mg/L (<5), high vaginal swab pending, urinalysis nil active

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Induction of labour with vaginal misoprostol now and intravenous benzylpenicillin given the unknown group B streptococcus status
Admit and give oral erythromycin 250 mg six hourly for ten days with antenatal betamethasone twice and expectant management to thirty four weeks
Outpatient management with twice weekly cardiotocograph reviews and serial inflammatory marker checks until thirty six weeks gestation
Tocolysis with nifedipine for 48 hours plus betamethasone, then discharge home for outpatient maternal-fetal medicine review
Emergency caesarean section now for imminent cord prolapse risk with immediate neonatal intensive care unit admission planning

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 attends antenatal clinic at 28+0 weeks for review of her routine gestational diabetes screening. She had a previous baby weighing 4.3 kg born at 40+1 weeks. Her booking BMI was 31 kg per square metre. She has no family history of type 2 diabetes and her first pregnancy did not require diabetes screening because of a different antenatal provider.

She completed a 75 g two-hour oral glucose tolerance test yesterday after an overnight fast. She is asymptomatic and her fetus is active. There is no glycosuria on urine dipstick today and her blood pressure is normal. She has no symptoms of polyuria or polydipsia. Her medications are routine pregnancy multivitamin only and she does not smoke. Her booking HbA1c was 5.4 percent.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 78, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L (target < 5.1), one hour 10.8 mmol/L (target < 10.0), two hour 8.6 mmol/L (target < 8.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that the oral glucose tolerance test is within normal range and review her at the routine 36 week appointment with no further action
Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test in four weeks because results are only marginally elevated and might normalise spontaneously
Commence insulin glargine 10 units at night and review with diabetes educator and dietitian once weekly until delivery and the postnatal review
Diagnose GDM, refer to diabetes educator and dietitian, start home blood glucose monitoring with fasting target under 5.1 and two hour postprandial under 6.7 mmol/L
Diagnose GDM and commence oral metformin 500 mg twice daily as first-line pharmacotherapy with dietitian review at the next clinic visit

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 at 38+2 weeks is in established labour in the delivery suite. The registrar performs an artificial rupture of membranes for slow progress. Cervix is 6 cm dilated, head is high at station minus one, contractions are three in ten and strong. Immediately after the artificial rupture of membranes the midwife observes a 6 cm length of umbilical cord prolapsing through the cervix into the vagina.

Fetal cardiotocograph immediately falls from a baseline of 140 to 80 with a flat trace. The mother is positioned supine on the bed. The emergency caesarean section is called overhead and the obstetric registrar arrives at the bedside within one minute. The anaesthetic team is paged and a theatre is being prepared on the floor below. The mother is calm but anxious and has had no opioid analgesia in the last six hours.

data_table.Vital signs: maternal pulse rate 96, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, fetal heart rate 80

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Replace the cord into the vagina manually with continuous fetal monitoring and proceed to ventouse-assisted vaginal delivery in the delivery suite
Position the mother left lateral, administer terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneously for tocolysis, and observe over five minutes
Elevate the presenting part with the examining hand, adopt knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position, and transfer immediately to theatre for emergency caesarean section
Apply suprapubic pressure with simultaneous fundal pressure and instruct the mother to push with each contraction for rapid vaginal delivery
Insert urinary catheter and instill 500 mL of saline to elevate the presenting part, then proceed to instrumental delivery in delivery suite

subtopic_detail: Severe HELLP delivery timing with steroid uncertainty
stem:
A 29-year-old G1P0 at 33+0 weeks is transferred to your tertiary delivery suite from a regional hospital with severe pre-eclampsia. She has had epigastric pain and nausea for 12 hours and her blood pressure has risen to 175/115 despite oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily. She has had no seizures. Fetal movements remain normal.

On examination she has right upper quadrant tenderness without peritonism and is alert (GCS 15) with hyperreflexia. Cardiotocograph is reactive, baseline 140, normal variability, no decelerations. Fetal estimated weight on ultrasound today is 1900 g (50th centile). Cervix is unfavourable on examination (Bishop score 2). Tertiary neonatal intensive care is available. Magnesium sulfate has been loaded and a labetalol infusion is running. No corticosteroid has yet been administered.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 108, blood pressure 168/108 on labetalol infusion, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, fetal heart rate 144 reactive
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-145, was 122 yesterday), platelets 78 x10^9/L (150-400, was 140 yesterday), ALT 312 U/L (was 80 yesterday), LDH 580 U/L (110-230), haptoglobin 0.1 g/L (0.3-2.0), peripheral blood film schistocytes present, urine protein:creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol, creatinine 92 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue magnesium sulfate and labetalol infusion and proceed to induction of labour with prostaglandin pessary targeting vaginal delivery within 24 hours
Continue magnesium sulfate and labetalol infusion plus give antenatal betamethasone and expectant management for 48 hours to complete the steroid course
Continue magnesium and labetalol infusion plus give antenatal betamethasone and intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg twice daily as treatment for HELLP itself
Continue magnesium and labetalol infusion, transfuse platelets to greater than 100, and book elective caesarean section in twelve hours after platelet recovery
Continue magnesium and labetalol infusion, give a first dose of antenatal betamethasone, and expedite caesarean section the same day without waiting for the second steroid dose

subtopic_detail: Ectopic with prior contralateral salpingectomy - historical-bilaterality flip
stem:
A 33-year-old G3P1 woman presents to the early pregnancy assessment unit with a positive urine pregnancy test, 6 weeks of amenorrhoea, right iliac fossa pain rated 5 out of 10, and minimal vaginal spotting. She is haemodynamically stable.

Her obstetric history includes a left tubal ectopic pregnancy three years ago managed by laparoscopic left salpingectomy, and a normal vaginal birth two years ago. She and her partner have been trying to conceive for 5 months and she very much hopes to have at least one more child.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a 28 mm right adnexal mass with a yolk sac and no fetal cardiac activity, and a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Beta-hCG today is 4800 IU/L. The right fallopian tube on prior imaging and intra-operative records from her left salpingectomy is structurally normal. There is no other contralateral pelvic pathology.

The gynaecology team is choosing between methotrexate medical management, laparoscopic right salpingostomy with tube preservation, and laparoscopic right salpingectomy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, no cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: TVUS as described; Hb 122 g/L (115-160); blood group A Rh positive; LFTs and renal function within normal limits
data_table.Past surgical history: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy three years ago; structurally normal right tube on prior records

lead_in: What would you first recommend as her definitive management?

options.text: Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m^2 intramuscularly with serial beta-hCG day 1, day 4, and day 7; expect more than 15 per cent fall in beta-hCG between day 4 and day 7
Laparoscopic right salpingostomy with linear incision over the antimesenteric border, evacuation of the ectopic, and haemostasis without tube removal, with serial beta-hCG follow-up
Laparoscopic right salpingectomy with removal of the affected tube, with counselling that future conception will require in vitro fertilisation (IVF) given the prior contralateral salpingectomy
Two-dose methotrexate protocol with methotrexate 50 mg/m^2 IM on day 0 and day 4, with serial beta-hCG day 1, day 4, day 7, and weekly until negative
Expectant management with weekly outpatient beta-hCG and TVUS, intervention reserved for failure to fall by more than 50 per cent at one week or for clinical deterioration
